author: jakobvogel
body:
### Description

Adds `ReceivedTokensTest`, covering how `ReceivedTokens.fromJson` determines the expiry of a refresh token. The method has four distinct outcomes, none of which was covered by a test so far:

- the expiry is read from the refresh token itself, if it is a JWT bearer token,
- it is derived from the access token lifetime, if that one outlives our default,
- it falls back to tomorrow for opaque tokens,
- or it stays empty if no refresh token was returned at all.

This also covers the sole usage of `com.auth0:java-jwt` in this project. The library appears in exactly one place (a single `JWT.decode` in `ReceivedTokens`), and that line was previously never executed by the build — so dependency bumps such as #1733 passed CI without exercising a single line of it.

No production code is touched. The tests deliberately pin the *current* behaviour, not a desired one.

### Additional Notes

- This PR fixes or works on following ticket(s): none, this is a drive-by improvement noticed while reviewing #1733.
- This PR is related to PR: #1733, and #1735 is stacked on top of it

### Two production issues found while writing this

Both predate this PR and are out of its scope, so they are fixed separately in #1735:

1. **NPE on a JWT without an `exp` claim.** In `ReceivedTokens:60`, `getExpiresAtAsInstant()` returns `null` for a structurally valid but `exp`-less JWT, so `.atZone(...)` throws a `NullPointerException`. That is not a `JWTDecodeException`, so it escapes the `catch` and aborts the whole token exchange instead of falling back to the default of tomorrow. Reproduced locally.
2. **Mixed time zones in one record.** `accessTokenExpiresAt` is a system-zone wall clock, while the JWT-derived `refreshTokenExpiresAt` is a UTC wall clock, and both are stored in `LocalDateTime` fields of the same record. On a host west of UTC the refresh token appears valid for longer than it is; east of UTC it appears to expire early. Our CI runs in UTC, which is why this is invisible there.

### Checklist

- [x] Code change has been tested and works locally
- [ ] Code was formatted via IntelliJ and follows SonarLint & [best practices](https://scireum.myjetbrains.com/youtrack/articles/MISC-A-16/CodeStyle-JavaDoc)
- [x] Patch Tasks: Is local execution of Patch Tasks necessary? If so, please also mark the PR with the tag. — not necessary, test-only change

The second box is intentionally left open: the IntelliJ formatter was run headlessly against `.idea/codeStyles/Project.xml` and reports *Formatted well*, but **SonarLint was not run** — it cannot be executed headlessly. Please run *Analyze VCS Changed Files* in the IDE before merging.

## What changed

Pricing page fixes on phones and tablets, plus content for the Korean home page.

**Pricing comparison table (below 1024px)**
- The plan switcher is a Noora button group instead of the hand-rolled dropdown it replaced (the real Noora dropdown teleports through LiveView portals, which never mount on this dead-rendered page). Selection toggles `data-selected` and the table's `.active` column.

author: matchascript
body:
On arm64 guests under Cloud Hypervisor the PCI host node is "pci@30000000",
so sysfs exposes /sys/devices/platform/30000000.pci/pci0000:00. The aarch64
root-bus lookup only accepted platform entries ending in ".pcie", fell back
to the QEMU virt path (4010000000.pcie) and then timed out waiting for
hotplug uevents there. Any virtio-blk hotplug on arm64 CLH failed this way;
block-mode emptyDir was the first path to hit it.

Match on the pci0000:<root complex> child directory instead of the entry
name suffix. The scan is factored into a helper with unit tests covering
the CLH and QEMU virt names.

Verified on x86_64: cargo test / fmt / clippy clean for the agent crate.

author: cirko33
body:
Closes #12949. Stacked on #13168 — review that first, this PR targets its branch.

## Flow

A request lives on the Coretime chain until it is accepted; only accepting asks the relay chain to open the channel. So a cancel never has to reach the relay chain to undo anything, and this whole call is CT-local:

1. Either end sends `hrmp_cancel_open_request` to the relay chain, which authenticates the asking para from the origin and forwards it to CT.
2. CT checks the witness, that the caller is one of the two ends, and that the request exists and has not been accepted.
3. The request is dropped, the sender's `OpenRequestCount` is decremented and its deposit is released. Only the sender can have paid, so `AcceptedRequestCount` is untouched.
4. The other end is told, via the relay chain, that the request is gone.

author: eddiedavison92
body:
Stacked on #1160. Applies the findings of a specification audit of all 105 NICE indicator measures, run as seven independent read-only reviews of the SQL and YAML against the published NICE indicator text.

## Audit result

| Verdict | Indicators |
|---|---|
| Match | 45 |
| Documented deviation (stated in the YAML) | 42 |
| Specification ambiguous | 6 |
| Wrong or undocumented gap, fixed here | 12 |

## Changes

- **IND229, IND274**: NICE sets no age range for the lipid-lowering primary prevention indicators; the 25 to 84 band is removed.
- **IND172**: NICE excludes under-18s and people with an unresolved diabetes diagnosis; both now applied.
- **Flu (IND131, IND141, IND163, IND164)**: `int_flu_vaccination_contraindication_all` now reads the persisting cluster XFLU_COD alongside the expiring FLUEXPCON_COD. A persisting contraindication excludes at any time, an expiring one in 12 months, as NICE words it. IND164 had no contraindication exclusion at all and now has one.
- **IND320**: the BMI model holds adult values only, so children in the denominator could never qualify; the denominator is now 18 and over and the description says so, along with the dyslipidaemia and NDH proxies.
- **Descriptions only**: IND88 (register entry read as the first diagnosis code), IND160 (the foot examination cluster is broader than the monofilament test NICE names), IND200 and IND202 (AUDIT counted as a positive screen alongside FAST and AUDIT-C), IND208 (falls discussion code stands for the three questions NICE lists).

## Left as documented readings, for the record

- SMI family applies the active-diagnosis population (excluding remission) to all 14 members, including the seven where NICE lists no remission exclusion and IND248 where NICE treats remission as a personalised care adjustment. Kept for consistency with the SMI programme; stated in every description.
- IND132 and IND133 do not apply NICE's antiplatelet and anticoagulant contraindication exclusions; the clusters exist and this is a candidate follow-up.
- IND104, IND265, IND266 keep the QOF age floors NICE does not set; IND266 counts an ethnicity category other than Unknown.
- IND143 cannot apply the relapse rule because relapse is not coded.
- IND173's NICE page contradicts itself on the diagnosis window.

## Checks

Built the affected chains in dev (81 nodes, all tests pass). Rates after the change: IND172 77%, IND229 56%, IND274 74%, IND320 61%, flu 52 to 60%.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Second pass: benchmark against published QOF

Compared every mapped indicator with NHS England's QOF 2025-26 achievement for the 174 NCL practices (gross rate: numerator over denominator plus personalised care adjustments, the closest analogue to a measure that applies no PCAs). 41 indicators are comparable; most sit within 10 points. Three further changes came out of it:

- **IND127**: the "previous score of 2 or more" exclusion applied to anyone ever scored, collapsing the denominator to ~4K against QOF's ~15K. It now applies only to people not reassessed in the period, as QOF AF006 reads it: denominator ~15K, 90% against QOF 95%.
- **IND191, IND195**: required an MRC grade, and NYHA plus a medication review, alongside the review code. QOF COPD010 and HF007 count the review code alone; heart failure read 32% against QOF 85%. Both now count the review code and carry the element dates as detail.

Systematic differences that remain and are not defects: NICE's "less than" against QOF's "or less" on the blood pressure targets (about six points at 140/90), and the March year-end review cycle, which in September leaves about 11% of the dementia and SMI registers with a plan 12 to 15 months old.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary

- Updated NICE indicator contracts to match the QOF 2025–26 benchmark.
- Removed unsupported age limits from IND229 and IND274.
- Added adult and unresolved-diagnosis exclusions to IND172.
- Added persisting and recent influenza contraindication handling for IND131, IND141, IND163 and IND164.
- Restricted IND320 to adults and documented proxy-measure limitations.
- Updated descriptions for IND88, IND160, IND200, IND202 and IND208.
- Changed IND127 to exclude only unreassessed prior high-risk scores.
- Changed IND191 and IND195 numerators to use review codes only. Related clinical dates remain reporting detail.

## Model and dependency changes

- The influenza contraindication model now emits persisting and expiring records. Its contract uses composite uniqueness across `id` and `source_cluster_id`.
- The atrial fibrillation profile now exposes `max_stroke_risk_score_before_period` for IND127.
- Downstream indicator population filters consume these new attributes. Other changes update existing filters and descriptions without introducing new model layers.

## Validation

- The affected development chains contain 81 nodes.
- All tests pass.

author: prageethw
body:
## Summary

Fixes issue #747: an orchestrator pane authored a task file intended for `delegate --task-file <path>` but never actually called `delegate` — the turn ended with the file sitting there unsent, and the pane looked ordinary-idle rather than stalled. A human had to notice and prompt the orchestrator twice.

A research pass into whether a mechanical deck-side safeguard is feasible found: no on-disk signal distinguishes a "pending" staging file from every other `.md` artifact already living in `.dot-agent-deck/` (reviewer/auditor findings, work-done reports, daemon-generated worker-task files), so both of the issue's own suggested heuristics would need new bookkeeping and would inherit real false-positive risk. After reviewing that research, decided to ship only the cheap, low-risk fix now — a self-check added to the orchestrator's own prompt — and revisit with real machinery only if this recurs.

## Change

`.dot-agent-deck.toml`: added a self-check to the orchestrator role's `prompt_template`, in the "Context handoff (CRITICAL)" bullet list, immediately after the existing task-file-staging instruction:

> Before ending your turn, confirm every task file you authored this turn for `--task-file` has a matching `delegate` call already issued in this same turn — a staged file with no `delegate` call behind it is a stalled task, not a finished one, and nothing on the deck notices the gap. If one is missing, issue the `delegate` call now, before you stop.

Scoped to the orchestrator role only (the only role that ever calls `delegate`) — since `anthropic`/`GPT` orchestrations both `extends = "mixed"` without overriding `prompt_template`, this one edit propagates to all three orchestrations.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features e2e -- -D warnings`, `cargo xtask linkage-check` all clean locally
- No `#[spec(...)]` test surface exists for a pure prompt-text change — `changelog.d/747.bugfix.md` carries a `No-Test:` line per `docs/develop/work-types.md`'s R3 escape hatch

author: kjothen
body:
`.tessl/` is gitignored, so every worktree Gas City creates starts without
`RULES.md` and without the plugin copies it links. `AGENTS.md` still imports
it, and the import resolves to nothing — an implementation worker has been
opening those trees with none of the ~27KB of guardrails the rules carry.

A session hook cannot close this: Claude Code loads memory *before* SessionStart
hooks run, so a file written then arrives a session too late. The repair has to
happen when the tree is created. Gas City's `prepare-worktree` step runs
`git worktree add`, and that fires `post-checkout` in the new tree — so the hook
reaches every worktree, agent-made or hand-made, without patching anything in
the pack.

## What changed

- `scripts/hooks/post-checkout` — on a branch or worktree checkout with no
  `.tessl/RULES.md`, runs `nix develop --command just tessl-plugins-install`.
  The dev shell is where `just` and `tessl` come from: nothing has allowed
  direnv in a tree that new, and an agent that ran `git worktree add` carries
  neither on its own PATH.
- `.envrc` — arms the hooks, and installs the rules when they are missing.
  Tracked hook scripts are inert until something copies them into the git dir,
  and that was previously a line in CLAUDE.md asking you to remember. The rules
  line covers the one tree `post-checkout` cannot: a clone's own checkout runs
  before there is any hook to run, so the primary checkout would otherwise stay
  bare while its worktrees were fine.
- `justfiles/dev.just` — `install-hooks` installs `post-checkout` alongside
  `pre-commit` and `commit-msg`, refuses to run from a linked worktree, and is
  silent unless a hook actually changed.
- `justfiles/tessl.just`, `CLAUDE.md` — the comments that explain the mechanism
  now say where a fresh worktree's copy comes from.

There is one hooks directory per clone, so one install covers every worktree,
including ones not created yet. That is also why a worktree must not be what
installs them: it would rewrite the hooks every other worktree runs, from
whatever commit a work item happened to land on.

The hook is advisory throughout: it never fails a checkout, and with neither nix
nor the tools available it warns and lets the checkout stand.

## Verified

On a fresh `git clone` of this branch, which is the state the bootstrap exists
for:

- the clone has no hooks and no `.tessl/`; the `.envrc` block installs three
  hooks and the rules in 6.6s, and every entry after that is 88ms and silent
- `just install-hooks` alone leaves `.tessl/` missing — which is why `.envrc`
  carries both lines
- editing one hook source re-installs exactly that one
- `just install-hooks` from a linked worktree refuses, names the primary
  checkout, and leaves the hooks dir byte-identical
- `git worktree add <path> --detach HEAD` — the exact form the formula runs —
  gives the new tree `.tessl/{RULES.md,PROFILE,plugins/}` with all five profile
  rule files resolving, in 8.2s
- `git status` in the new worktree is clean; everything written is gitignored
- run separately with `tessl` absent from PATH entirely, the install still lands
- a re-checkout in an already-populated tree is 27ms, so the guard costs a stat

body: ## Why OpenAI's speech path is now GPT-Live-1. Walle still spoke through `gpt-realtime-2.1`. Live has no input commit and no end-of-reply event, so a model-string swap would leave the device without `turn.done`. Firmware and protocol v1 stay frozen. Hold-to-speak, 24 kHz PCM16, exact `outputSamples`, and local fallback until the first remote codec write are unchanged. ## Scope - Pure turn reducer in `cloud/src/live-turn.ts`. Capture (`open | holding | sealed`) is separate from stream (`quiet | awaiting | voicing | orphaned`). - `OpenAILiveSession` talks to `https://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions`. First event is `session.start` with `gpt-live-1`, `audio/pcm` at 24000, voice `ballad`, and `WALLE_LIVE_INSTRUCTIONS`. - Device PCM is held locally. `turn.commit` bursts `unmute`, chunked `session.input_audio.append`, then `mute`. If an earlier reply is still draining, the burst waits until the stream is quiet. - A reply ends 1200 ms after the last output audio or transcript delta. `onDone` reports every forwarded sample, including the tail. Frames before the last are 1920 bytes. - `response.cancel` orphans the tail. A new `turn.start` during a reply fails the old turn with `superseded`. - Personality version is `walle-warm-curious-v3`. The long-form reference prompt is not sent. - `cloud/src/openai-realtime.ts` is deleted. `WalleAgent` still uses the same three-line connect surface. ## Tradeoffs Burst-on-commit over stream-during-hold. Live is full duplex. Streaming while the user holds would let a pause mid-hold start a reply that then concatenates with later speech. Quiet-gap end detection. Live has no speech `response.done`. 1200 ms is a guess. Too short truncates. Too long delays `turn.done`. Live-phase provider errors fault the claimed turn and keep the socket. A starting-phase error still rejects `connect` and falls back to echo. A mid-session voice rejection should not tear the socket down. ## Blast radius Cloud relay only. Device protocol, firmware, and Agent SQLite schema are unchanged. `hibernate: false` is unchanged. No `openai` npm package. Connect failure falls back to echo. Socket loss after `session.started` closes the device with 1012 so firmware reconnects. Bring-up, not proven on a device or against live OpenAI: - Burst plus immediate mute may not elicit speech. If it does not, `firstAudioMs` fails closed at 6 s with `no_upstream_audio` and the device uses local fallback. - Voice `ballad` may be rejected on Live. That rejects `connect` and falls back to echo. - `turn.cancelled` for a superseded non-current turn id increments firmware `protocol_errors` and is otherwise ignored. ## Verification Matching surface is the adapter. There are no Agent integration tests. ``` cd cloud && npm run typecheck && npm test ``` 5 files, 44 tests, typecheck clean. Covers hold/commit/burst/deltas/`onDone` with exact samples, cancel mid-hold, cancel after commit, `begin` during voicing, late deltas after `onDone`, `session.start` JSON, and connect-phase errors that never fire `onUnavailable`. Not verified: a live OpenAI session, or a physical hold-to-speak on the ESP32.

author: dgnaglo
body:
Deux corrections, mesurées ce matin sur l'image republiée.

## 1. `perl-base` — les trois dernières critiques

L'image `apowerb/th2pulse:0.1.4` republiée à 08:09 tourne bien sur **Debian 13.6**, mais elle garde **trois vulnérabilités critiques**, toutes sur le même paquet :

| CVE | paquet | correctif |
|---|---|---|
| CVE-2026-13221 | `perl-base` | aucun |
| CVE-2026-42496 | `perl-base` | aucun |
| CVE-2026-8376 | `perl-base` | aucun |

`th2etl` était dans la même situation hier et a purgé ce paquet (PR #22). Résultat mesuré par digest ce matin : **`th2etl:0.0.12` est à zéro critique**, contre cinq avant.

La justification vaut à l'identique ici : `perl-base` arrive comme paquet **Essential** de `python:3.11-slim-trixie`, cette image n'installe **aucun paquet système**, et son `CMD` est `python -m th2pulse`. Rien n'appelle perl.

Pour qui étend l'image : `apt-get install` continue de fonctionner pour les paquets ordinaires, et un paquet dont les scripts de maintenance sont écrits en Perl le réinstallera comme n'importe quelle dépendance manquante.

## 2. Un défaut de ma PR #8 — `latest` peut reculer

En reprenant le `workflow_dispatch` de `th2etl`, j'ai repris le déclencheur **sans reprendre sa garde sur `latest`**. Ici les deux tags sont poussés dans tous les cas :

```yaml
tags: |
  apowerb/th2pulse:${{ steps.release.outputs.version }}
  apowerb/th2pulse:latest
```

Conséquence : republier une version **antérieure** — reconstruire `0.1.2` sur une base corrigée, exactement l'usage que #8 rendait possible — ferait **reculer `latest`**, et toute installation qui ne fixe pas le tag suivrait la descente sans le moindre signal.

`th2etl` protège explicitement contre ça, avec un commentaire qui dit pourquoi. Je l'aligne : `latest` ne bouge plus que sur un enchaînement de release.

## Vérification

Le smoke test du workflow exerce l'image après le build — c'est lui qui dira si l'application démarre encore sans perl. Un essai à blanc (`publish` décoché) permet de le jouer sur cette branche avant de merger.

Ensuite, l'oracle est un scan **par digest** de l'image reconstruite. Jamais par tag : hier, le cache de trivy m'a servi le digest de `latest` à la place de l'image que je croyais mesurer, et j'ai failli conclure que la republication n'avait rien changé.

body:
Comment-only follow-up to #86 (code review findings).

- `Kconfig.sysbuild`: the merged comment claimed the mcuboot child "picks up its board-specific config from mcuboot.conf in this directory" — wrong: NCS sysbuild never puts board-dir `mcuboot.conf` on the child's CONF_FILE chain (PlatformIO-build convention only; verified against the child's CONF_FILE in a sysbuild build). The child's board config actually comes from the `if MCUBOOT` defaults in `Kconfig.xiao_nrf54lm20b` / `Kconfig.defconfig`. Aligned the comment with that mechanism.
- `mcuboot.conf`: header made the matching false claim ("automatically loaded by Zephyr sysbuild"); now documents the PlatformIO-only scope and points NCS users at the Kconfig defaults.
- `Kconfig.sysbuild`: added a warning that the rebuilt mcuboot child is a signing-config artifact, **not** the factory bootloader (no Button-0 debounce, no serial) — `west flash` over a debug probe must not program it over the factory bootloader; applications are updated via USB DFU (`zephyr.signed.bin`).

No code/Kconfig behavior changes.

body:
Ein Klick auf das Logo im Kopfbereich rückte die Seite nur ein Stück nach oben, statt an den Anfang zu springen.

## Ursache

Der Anker saß auf dem **klebenden Kopfbereich** (`position: sticky`). Weil der beim Scrollen oben festklebt, hält der Browser ihn für bereits sichtbar und rückt beim Ankersprung nur um die Höhe von `scroll-padding-top` nach.

Gemessen: 546 px am Rechner, 518 px am Handy — statt an den Seitenanfang.

Der Anker liegt jetzt auf `<body>`, das nicht klebt.

## Dieselbe Falle in zwei Demos

| | vorher | jetzt |
|---|---|---|
| Firmenseite | 8.064 px | 0 px |
| HAARSCHARF. | 0 px | 0 px |
| Frisörsalon Wenzel | 76 px | 0 px |
| Sonnenwerk | 169 px | 0 px |

HAARSCHARF war von Anfang an richtig. Bei Wenzel und Sonnenwerk lag der Anker unter Kopf- und Hinweisleiste — die in PR #24 ergänzte Hinweisleiste hat den Versatz dort zusätzlich vergrößert.

## Sonderfall Sonnenwerk

Dort trägt `#top` zusätzlich den Sprunglink „Zum Inhalt springen". Der muss am Menü vorbeiführen und bleibt deshalb auf `<main>`; der Markenlink hat ein eigenes Ziel bekommen. Ein blindes Verschieben hätte die Tastaturbedienung beschädigt.

Auf den Unterseiten ist der Zusatz `index.html#top` ersatzlos entfallen — ein frischer Seitenaufruf beginnt ohnehin oben, und das Fragment führte dort sogar unter den Hero-Bereich.

Alle fünf Sprunglinks führen weiterhin korrekt zum Inhaltsbereich.

author: jimwei
body:
## 背景

Codex 定时任务 / 心跳（Schedule、automation heartbeat）在首轮响应之后再次投递时，会带上 `previous_response_id`，并把 `automation_update` 的 `<heartbeat>`（或普通 Automation 元数据）作为**孤立的 `function_call_output`** 放进 `input`。该输出承载的是下一轮任务的指令，请求里并没有与之配对的调用项。

线上（本仓库部署的 api.gccode.cn）实测该形状会被上游 HTTP Responses 拒绝：

```
POST /v1/responses
{"model":"deepseek-v4-flash","previous_response_id":"resp_xxx","input":[
  {"type":"function_call_output","id":"fco_ct","name":"automation_update","namespace":"codex_app",
   "output":"<heartbeat>\n  <automation_id>test</automation_id>\n  <instructions>\nReply with exactly CT_OK\n  </instructions>\n</heartbeat>"}]}

→ 400 {"error":{"message":"Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: input: missing field `call_id` at line 1 column 294"}}
```

不带 `previous_response_id` 的同类请求会被 `normalizeCodexAutomationBootstrap` 改写成 user 消息并正常返回 200；但续写路径被 `allowHistoricalContext=false` 提前挡住，未做归一化就直通上游，于是失败（HTTP 续写不支持孤立的 `function_call_output`，只有 Responses WebSocket v2 支持）。

## 改动

- `normalizeCodexAutomationBootstrap` 现在与 delegation 一致地允许在 `previous_response_id` 续写上完成改写；两个开关（历史上下文 / 续写）拆成 `codexBootstrapNormalizeOptions` 的具名字段，调用点意图更清晰。
- 安全边界保持不变：请求内出现真实调用项、输出带非空 `call_id`、命名空间不是 `codex_app`、信封/元数据校验不通过等情况依旧不改写。

## 测试

- 新增 `TestNormalizeCodexAutomationBootstrapPreviousResponseID`：续写请求改写为 `user` 消息、保留 `previous_response_id`、可重入（第二次调用不再改写）。
- 新增 `TestNormalizeCodexAutomationBootstrapPreviousResponseIDWithCallContext`：续写请求中存在真实调用项时不改写（负例）。
- 原有「previous response 属于不安全形状」的用例相应移除，其余不安全形状用例保持不变。

## 验证

```
cd backend && go test -tags=unit ./internal/handler/... -count=1
ok  github.com/Wei-Shaw/sub2api/internal/handler  38.992s
cd backend && go build ./...
（无输出）
```

单元层面已覆盖；改写后的请求形状与已经验证可用的非续写路径完全一致。

PO VISUAL APPROVAL: GRANTED.

Canonical user avatar met eigen profielfoto: kiezen, user-controlled 1:1 crop (pan+zoom), vervangen en verwijderen, met initialen-fallback.

**Datamodel** atleet_profiel.avatar_path bewaart een storage-PAD, geen URL. Private bucket avatars (2MB, jpeg/png/webp, geen SVG) met vier owner-bound policies die het eerste padsegment tegen auth.uid() toetsen; nul policies voor anon.

**Replace** upload (immutable uuid-key) -> canonical write op alleen avatar_path -> pas daarna oude object opruimen; mislukte write rolt het nieuwe object terug en laat de bestaande avatar intact. Geen Date.now()-cachebuster.

**Erasure** beide verwijderpaden ruimen de storage-objecten op.

**Migratie v562 is reeds toegepast op PRODUCTIE** (mhfxhzkdmgkaplicdszg). Read-only geverifieerd: additief, niet-brekend, inert (0 van 4 rijen gebruikt de kolom). Geen rollback. Procesbevinding vastgelegd: productiemigraties achter een PO-gate vereisen voortaan expliciete goedkeuring vooraf.

**Security evidence: STRUCTURAL/POLICY PROVEN (C) + AUTHENTICATED-RLS VALIDATION OPEN.** Cross-user en unauthenticated write zijn NIET end-to-end bewezen; daarvoor is een authenticated-user oracle nodig. Dit blokkeert de PR niet maar mag niet als volledige RLS-certificering worden gepresenteerd.

author: mwh-max
body:
## Summary

- `script.js` had grown to 743 lines covering date display, streak tracking, the share-card modal, eco-action selection, the counter, custom tasks, and notifications — all as a single non-module script relying on implicit `window` globals.
- Split it into feature modules along natural seams: `ui-helpers.js`, `date-display.js`, `streak-display.js`, `share-card.js`, `eco-actions.js`, `count-tracker.js`, `custom-tasks.js`, `notifications.js`. `script.js` is now a ~150-line entry point that wires the modules together and owns page lifecycle (`initUI`, `resetApp`, `refreshAfterSync`).
- `script.js` is now loaded as a real ES module (`<script type="module">`), consistent with `lib.js`/`auth.js`/`sync.js`/`supabase-client.js`. Modules `import`/`export` explicitly instead of relying on `window` globals for internal wiring; removed `lib.js`'s `window.parseJSON`/etc. exposure since it existed only to support the old non-module `script.js`.
- `window.resetApp`/`window.setupAuth`/`window.sync` stay as-is — that's the genuine cross-module contract with `auth.js`/`sync.js`.
- Updated `sw.js`'s cache manifest (new files + bumped cache version) and `index.html`'s script tag accordingly.
- Fixed `eslint.config.js`: it set `sourceType: 'script'` project-wide, which failed to parse every file using `import`/`export` (including files that predate this change). Defaulted to `sourceType: 'module'` with an override for `sw.js` (a classic worker script).
- Ran `eslint --fix` and hand-cleaned the remaining pre-existing style violations (`curly`, `quotes`, `comma-dangle`) across the repo, including files untouched by the module split.

## Test plan

- [x] `vitest run` — 45/45 passing
- [x] `eslint .` — 0 errors, 0 warnings
- [x] Headless-browser smoke test (Playwright) exercising the full module import graph — date display, streak dots, and an end-to-end eco-action click through `eco-actions.js` → `streak-display.js` — output verified byte-identical to the pre-refactor baseline
- [x] Same smoke test re-run against `main` to confirm no behavior changed

> Stacked on #90 — review only the latest commit. Base retargets to `main` once #90 merges.
>
> Backend half is tiket-bisa/tiketbisa-be#110. This PR is safe to merge on its own: the SDK-key refresh simply stays null until that lands.

## Problem

At step 4/4 the QRIS/VA sometimes never renders — the buyer sees `Pembayaran belum dapat dimuat. Silakan coba lagi.` above a permanently disabled `Buat Nomor Virtual Account`, or a QR stuck loading. Nothing on the screen can recover it, so support has been handling these over WhatsApp.

## Root cause

Three independent defects, each on its own sufficient to produce that screen:

1. **The failure is terminal in the UI.** `fatal-error` set the error text but nothing re-created the `XenditComponents` instance, and the submit button is `disabled={!ready}` — `ready` only flips on the SDK's `submission-ready` event, which never arrives. The effect is keyed on `componentsSdkKey`, which never changes, so nothing re-runs. `Cek Status Pembayaran` is also hidden in this state because `awaitingConfirmation` is false. The buyer is looking at a dead screen.
2. **The status poll could never heal it.** `getTransactionStatus` and `getOrderById` did not parse `componentsSdkKey`, so neither the 5 s poll nor a page reload could ever recover a Components-mode session.
3. **The auto-create was one-shot.** `gatewayInvoiceRequestedRef` is claimed *before* the await and was never released on failure, so a single transient `executeOrder` error was permanent for that lock. Its guard also ignored `componentsSdkKey`, so a perfectly good Components order was treated as having nothing to show.

## Change

- A `Muat Ulang Pembayaran` button appears whenever the SDK reports an error, re-mounting the session via a `reloadToken` in the effect deps. Covers both `fatal-error` and the `QRIS belum tersedia` branch.
- `componentsSdkKey` is parsed in `getTransactionStatus` and `getOrderById`, so the existing poll can now hand the component a fresh key.
- The auto-create guard treats an SDK key as renderable, and releases the ref in its `catch` so retry genuinely re-fires.

## Testing

`pnpm typecheck` clean. `pnpm vitest run app/modules/external/checkout` — 61 passed, including a new case asserting a fatal error surfaces the retry button and that clicking it constructs a second `XenditComponents` instance.

The real gateway failure path needs live Xendit credentials and is not reproducible locally; the ranking above is from code reading, not production logs. The backend PR adds the logging that will confirm which defect buyers actually hit.

author: guillaume-chervet
body:
Fixes duplicated or misdirected Traffic animations during cold starts, publications, recursive function calls and queued HTTP processing. Each synchronous request follows caller → SlimFaas → selected replica → SlimFaas → caller. A publication arrives once and fans out once per destination.

Internal calls resolve the exact caller pod from SlimFaas's inventory. Managed native functions use signed per-replica gateways because their processes share loopback. A single Fibonacci recursive POST therefore has one External arrival and one final External response; its 286 internal calls and replies stay between SlimFaas and the known Fibonacci pods.

Queue attempts retain their correlation through logical completion and HTTP 202 callbacks. The canvas draws one reply from the executing replica to its queue; technical HTTP responses remain in the journal. Playback preserves ordering even when dequeue/send aliases arrive in reverse order. The SSE shape, AOT serialization and WebSocket client protocol are unchanged.

Adds a three-node native Playwright CI suite using real Fibonacci processes. Five scenarios observe real SSE and canvas coordinates, shapes, colors and aggregation counters from the receiving node and a peer: controlled cold start, two-replica publication, recursion with input 12 (result 144, 287 invocations), async HTTP completion, and a real callback held behind a test gate. Existing keyboard, mobile and reduced-motion checks remain. The readiness endpoint test now observes the waiting event, releases a ready snapshot explicitly, and asserts the dispatch target within a bounded deadline instead of relying on runner speed. Documentation includes reproduction commands and captures.

Validation:
- Full .NET suite: 1,465 tests passed.
- Dashboard: 54 tests; production and Storybook builds passed.
- Native Playwright: all five scenarios passed twice locally on macOS ARM64 and passed on Linux CI.
- Native AOT publication and documentation site build passed (21 pages, 1,376 local links/assets).
- Native local demo: manifest validation, status and Hello local function smoke passed with temporary state.
- AOT async load smoke: 4,292 requests in five seconds, zero failures, 12 concurrent callers, dashboard enabled (858 requests/s, p95 18.9 ms). This is a short smoke check, not a comparative benchmark.

Playwright 1.63.0 remains pinned with its lockfile. CI installs Chromium through the local locked Playwright binary, addressing the SonarCloud alerts about `npx`. On commit `4564e7be`, the .NET and dashboard tests, all five native Playwright scenarios, documentation, SonarCloud analysis and quality gate, DCO, FOSSA License Compliance, and all five native publication targets have passed. The Docker image build also passed: all 27 applicable checks are successful (7 checks are skipped on this PR).

CI results: [dashboard and native Playwright](https://github.com/SlimPlanet/SlimFaas/actions/runs/34595354225), [full CI and native publications](https://github.com/SlimPlanet/SlimFaas/actions/runs/34595354326).

Kubernetes pod attribution is covered by backend tests; no live Kubernetes cluster was used locally. Independently launched `debugUrl` processes do not receive automatic environment rewriting.

Closes #352

author: keyfire
body:
Every process this repository starts is read as text and names `encoding="utf-8"` - and nowhere was that written down, and nothing checked it. A new script then broke the rule, and the failure was the silent kind: the output of a generator naming the Russian pages it writes was decoded with the code page of the console, the names came back as replacement characters, the text was lost, and the exit code went on saying the run had gone well.

The convention now lives in `CLAUDE.md`, with both of its halves. The reader names the encoding (and `errors="replace"` where the output only goes to a human). The child has to write what the reader reads: a plain Python script encodes its own stream with that same code page, so a script started from here is given `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` - the elemctl CLI reconfigures its streams itself, a script does not. A call that asks for no text at all decodes nothing and needs neither.

`tests/test_conventions.py` reads `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `tools` with `ast`. With `ast` rather than a regular expression on purpose: the offending call is written `(run or subprocess.run)(...)`, so a check reading the head of a call would have looked straight past the one case that started this.

Before: two findings - `tests/test_build.py:659` (a git helper, which captures file names) and `tests/test_cli.py:65`, both decoding with the code page of the machine. Both fixed, and the check is green. Full suite: 497 passed; `python scripts/check_docs.py` green.

author: carstvaartjes
body:
## Why

The web library was just given server-side `sort` and `updated_since` controls (#691), and its own tests prove the browser **sends** them. Nothing proved the **server honours** them: the projection's tests only ever used default ordering, so "sorting and recency filtering work" rested on reading the implementation.

That is exactly the gap worth closing — a control that sends a parameter nobody applies would look correct in the UI and quietly mislead.

## What this adds

One new test file, `control/tests/test_library_sort_recency.py`, with a five-test corpus. It is **test-only**: nothing under `control/src/` changed, because the investigation found **no defect** — both `sort` values and `updated_since` are genuinely honoured.

Design notes that make it evidence rather than restatement:

- A small synthetic corpus (3 models + 3 recipes) built from `catalog-index.json` templates, with a **clock that advances between inserts** so `updated_at` ordering is deterministic. Slugs are chosen so **name order and recency order differ** (`alpha, bravo, charlie` vs `bravo, alpha, charlie`).
- The decisive assertion is `name_order != updated_order` — **the one that fails if `sort` is ignored**. Without it, an implementation that ignores the parameter would pass every ordering check.
- The identity **sets** must match across orderings, so sorting cannot silently drop or duplicate entries.
- `updated_since` is exercised with a cutoff that drops the oldest entry, an inclusive-boundary case at exactly the surviving timestamp, and a check that facets are unaffected.
- A cursor issued under one ordering and reused under the other **is rejected**, pinned in both directions for both routes: the sort is embedded in the cursor context (`library_projection.py:702`, `:882`) and `CursorCodec.decode` raises `ValueError("cursor is invalid")` on a context mismatch (`auth.py:359,363-364`).
- An unknown sort raises `ValueError` from the projection itself.

## Fail-first

Demonstrated without touching production code, using a throwaway pytest plugin that replaces `_model_sort_key`/`_recipe_sort_key` with a constant:

```
4 failed, 1 passed in 0.20s
assert name_order != updated_order
AssertionError: assert ['test/charlie', 'test/alpha', 'test/bravo'] != ['test/charlie', 'test/alpha', 'test/bravo']
```

Only the unknown-sort test survives that mutation, which is correct.

## Verification

- New file: **5 passed in 0.48s**.
- `control/tests/test_library_canonical_projection.py` (untouched): 3 passed.
- **Control fast tier: 1832 passed, 2 skipped** — and with the new file ignored, 1827 passed, 2 skipped. So the tier gained five tests and **no measurable wall time**; this does not become the next bottleneck.
- `pyright` on the new file: **0 errors, 0 warnings**. `ruff check`: clean.
- No new dependency, no production change, no existing assertion altered.

author: chizhangucb
body:
Closes #185

`hold` was read only by the dispatcher. Now the retry handler and the reconciler read the same hold set from `factory/lib/labels.ts`, so a person who adds `hold` to a ticket already in flight stops the factory starting anything more on it. A cancel with `hold` gets no replacement; a bare cancel still gets one, exactly as before.

## What changed

- **Retry handler** (`decide.ts`, `retry.ts`): `findHold` reads `HOLD_LABELS` on the ticket, then on its open PR. A hit makes `decide` answer `stand-down`, which:
  - writes no `agent:implement`, no `factory:retry-N`, no `needs-human`, and takes no `agent:*` off
  - comments on the subject the hold was found on, naming the label and the subject
  - leaves the subject where a requeue leaves one (#148): a ticket with no factory label for the dispatcher, a PR kept in `agent:in-progress` (via `keepInProgress`) for the reconciler
- **Reconciler** (`reconcile.ts`, `sweep.ts`): a held ticket, a held PR, and a PR whose ticket is held are left alone and logged `held: <label>`. That covers the stuck path and the merge rules alike, as parking already does. `PARKED_LABELS` is unchanged. `sweep.ts` skips reads for held subjects through the new `leftAlone`.
- **Docs**: `docs/agents/hold.md` rewritten for in-flight work. ADR 0005 gets a dated correction on the `hold` bullet. `labels.ts` doc comments, `pipeline.md`'s two hold sentences, and CONTEXT.md (the Hold entry, plus a new **Stand-down** entry) are updated.

## The three design points

**1. Where the hold check sits: at the top of `decide`, right after `escalated`.** It comes ahead of requeue, hand-off, unretryable and the retry cap.
- Escalation takes every `agent:*` label and `ready-for-agent` off and puts `needs-human` on. That is the factory reclaiming a subject a person just took, and it leaves a state that removing `hold` can't resume from. So a held subject whose retry is spent stands down. Pinned: "a held subject whose retry is spent stands down rather than escalating", on every failure kind, plus the unretryable and conflict cases.
- A hand-off starts an agent too, so it also yields to the hold.
- `escalated` stays first: nothing to do, and no second comment.

**2. What "held" means to the reconciler: the whole `HOLD_LABELS` set, read beside `PARKED_LABELS` rather than inside it.**
- Whole set, not `hold` alone. The retry handler stands down on all three labels (AC1). A reconciler that re-stamped on `needs-triage` or `ready-for-human` would undo that stand-down at its next deadline. On a PR it's worse: re-stamp, review fails, stand down again, and the second miss escalates, which is the one outcome #185 rules out.
- Not inside `PARKED_LABELS`. CONTEXT.md's **Parked** is "always the factory's own doing, which is what separates it from a **hold**", and ADR 0005 says `PARKED_LABELS` "is exactly the pair". So the behaviour is parking's (nothing repaired), and the log says `held: hold`, the word the dispatcher already logs for the same label. AC4 says "reported as parked"; I read that as the behaviour, and the glossary decides the word. A test pins `PARKED_LABELS` as the pair.
- A PR counts as held when the ticket it closes is held, for the same loop reason: the handler reads both.
- Consequence, named in hold.md: `needs-triage` or `ready-for-human` on a PR the factory is working on now stops it. A target whose automation labels PRs `needs-triage` holds every factory PR it touches.

**3. The resume path. The brief's premise holds for PRs, not for tickets.**
- **Ticket:** `agent-implement.yml` drops `agent:implement` in "Transition labels" and `agent:in-progress` in the retry job a step *before* the handler runs. So a stood-down ticket carries no `agent:*` label, the reconciler has nothing to sweep, and the **dispatcher** resumes it once the hold comes off. That happens at once on the `unlabeled` wake, or within the heartbeat's 10 minutes if the event is lost. It spends no reconciler miss. A test pins the workflow facts and `whySkipped` before and after.
- **PR, or a ticket held with its start label still on:** the **reconciler's** stuck path, on its first sweep past `stuck_minutes`. The deadline runs from when the start label went on, not from when the hold came off, so work held longer than 15 min resumes on the next sweep. Pinned by "removing the hold resumes a held subject through the stuck path". hold.md says so, and also that the resume counts as the reconciler's first miss, as a requeue's does.
- **AC5 needs rewording** on the issue ("through the reconciler's existing stuck path" is true for PRs, not tickets), much as #170's AC3 did.

## What it still doesn't stop

These are all named in hold.md, `labels.ts` and ADR 0005, and are outside this ticket's files:
- **An agent workflow's own success step.** Implement and implement-pr both label their PR `agent:review` on success, so a run already going when the hold lands still gets reviewed, and can merge on a pass. Cancel the run to stop that.
- **update-branch's `planConflict`.** It hands a conflicting, armed, factory-authored PR with no `agent:*` label to the implementer, held or not, and also when its ticket is held. A stood-down PR keeps `agent:in-progress` and is already skipped there.
- **A cancel before the implementer step starts.** The step's outcome reads as skipped or empty, not `cancelled`, so the handler exits 1 before deciding, and the workflow's fallback adds `agent:blocked`, as today. No agent starts; removing `hold` doesn't resume it, and re-adding `agent:implement` does.
- **Auto-merge.** A hold doesn't disarm auto-merge that's already armed.

These look worth a follow-up ticket each.

## Criterion 6 is unchanged

`isImplementerFailure` still reads `cancelled` as the implementer's failure. Pinned: "a cancel with no hold gets exactly one bounded replacement, as before #185", which passes on the merge-base.

## Mutation checks

Each guard was broken by hand, went red on the test named for it, and was restored byte-identically with `git checkout`:

| Mutation | Went red |
|---|---|
| retry handler drops `held` from its `decide` call | "asks the hold set before it decides": "decide is never told about the hold it found" |
| `decide`'s hold branch disabled | the two stand-down tests |
| held subject escalates once its retry is spent | "stands down rather than escalating": `implement, retry spent`, actual `escalate` |
| reconciler ignores held on the stuck path | held ticket, held PR, resume tests |
| reconciler ignores a PR's ticket hold | held-PR and merge-rule tests |
| reconciler reads `hold` alone | whole-set, merge-rule and parked-pair tests |
| merge rules ignore held | "neither judged nor re-armed" |
| stand-down drops `keepInProgress` | "standing down writes no retry label..." |
| `hold` added to `PARKED_LABELS` | 4 tests, the logs turning `parked:` |
| stand-down writes a retry label | "standing down writes no retry label..." |
| `findHold` ignores the PR | "findHold reads the whole hold set..." |

## Skills invoked

- `mattpocock-skills:tdd` (vertical slices: `decide`, `findHold`, the comment, `retry.ts` wiring, the dispatcher resume, the reconciler). `mattpocock-skills:implement` is disable-model-invocation, so its steps were followed with `tdd` loaded directly.
- `mattpocock-skills:code-review` against the merge-base, with #185 as the spec. Fixes are in the `review:` commit.
- bundled `code-review medium --fix`: ran clean, no findings and no edits, so no commit for it. It noted two pre-existing edges it left alone: a hold added between the sweep's snapshot and its apply can still be re-stamped (parked subjects share that window), and a hold on the PR alone gets its comment on the PR only.

## Proof

- `npm run typecheck`: clean
- `npm test`: 511 pass, 0 fail, against 498 on `main` at `1157c26` (+13, all new tests in `decide.test.ts` and `reconcile.test.ts`)

## ADRs

Nothing here contradicts an ADR once ADR 0005's correction is in. The old "tickets only" and "dispatcher al

author: gauranshahuja
body:
### Issue # (if applicable)

Closes #34296.

### Reason for this change

`Subnet` (and `PublicSubnet`/`PrivateSubnet`) require a concrete `cidrBlock`, while `AWS::EC2::Subnet` can allocate its IPv4 CIDR from an Amazon VPC IP Address Manager pool (`Ipv4IpamPoolId` + `Ipv4NetmaskLength`). `Vpc` already supports IPAM for the VPC CIDR through `IpAddresses.awsIpamAllocation()`, but a standalone L2 subnet cannot use IPAM without dropping to the L1, or overriding the L1 properties with `CfnSubnetPropsMixin` and a placeholder `cidrBlock`.

### Description of changes

- `SubnetProps.cidrBlock` becomes optional and a new optional `ipv4IpamAllocation: SubnetIpamAllocation` prop is added, where `SubnetIpamAllocation` is `{ ipamPool: IIPAMPoolRef, netmaskLength: number }`.
- `Subnet` validates that exactly one of `cidrBlock`/`ipv4IpamAllocation` is set and that `netmaskLength` is within /16 to /28 (the IPv4 subnet sizes the package already enforces in `NetworkBuilder`; skipped for tokens), using `ValidationError` with `lit` codes.
- `Ipv4IpamPoolId`/`Ipv4NetmaskLength` are passed to `CfnSubnet`. When IPAM is used, `subnet.ipv4CidrBlock` is `CfnSubnet.attrCidrBlock` (a deploy-time token) instead of a concrete string, the same way `Vpc.vpcCidrBlock` is `attrCidrBlock` for an IPAM-allocated VPC.
- README: new "Allocating a subnet CIDR from AWS IPAM" section.

Design decisions, flagged for review:

1. Nested struct rather than flat `ipv4IpamPoolId`/`ipv4NetmaskLength`: the two values are only valid together (co-dependent props rule in `docs/AGENTS_CONSTRUCT_DESIGN.md`). Exclusivity with the pre-existing `cidrBlock` cannot be made structural without adding a second, factory-style way to express the CIDR, so it is validated at construction time as proposed in the issue.
2. `ipamPool: IIPAMPoolRef` rather than an ID string, following the preference for `I*Ref` interfaces in props (as in `placementGroup?: IPlacementGroupRef`, `networkAcl: INetworkAclRef`). `CfnIPAMPool` implements it directly and `CfnIPAMPool.fromIpamPoolId()` covers pools created elsewhere. `AwsIpamProps.ipv4IpamPoolId` is still a `string` (with a "todo: should be a type" comment); happy to switch to a string if consistency with it is preferred.
3. `netmaskLength` is required, mirroring `AwsIpamProps.ipv4NetmaskLength`; relaxing it to optional later is non-breaking.
4. Not implemented as a mixin: the blocker is the L2 props contract (`cidrBlock` required, `ipv4CidrBlock` derived from it), which a mixin must not change. `CfnSubnetPropsMixin` remains the escape hatch, e.g. for IPv6 IPAM allocation, which is left for a follow-up.
5. Consumers of `ipv4CidrBlock` that parse the CIDR (`SubnetFilter.byCidrMask()`, `byCidrRanges()`, `containsIpAddresses()`) cannot work with a deploy-time value; this is documented on the prop and in the README rather than changed. Subnets created by `Vpc` from `subnetConfiguration` are untouched.
6. Making `cidrBlock` optional on an input struct is source-compatible for callers; `PublicSubnetProps`/`PrivateSubnetProps` inherit the new prop.

Alternatives considered and rejected: flat props (co-dependent rule); a `SubnetIpAddresses.cidr()/.ipam()` factory prop mirroring `Vpc.ipAddresses` (`cidrBlock` already exists and cannot be removed); optional `netmaskLength` using the pool's default netmask as in #34349 (deferred).

### Describe any new or updated permissions being added

None. No IAM policies are created; the allocation uses the deploying principal's existing EC2/IPAM permissions.

### Description of how you validated changes

- Unit tests in `packages/aws-cdk-lib/aws-ec2/test/vpc.test.ts` (`describe('Subnet')`): the concrete-CIDR path renders exactly as before (`CidrBlock`, no IPAM properties); the IPAM path renders `Ipv4IpamPoolId`/`Ipv4NetmaskLength` and no `CidrBlock`, both with `CfnIPAMPool.fromIpamPoolId()` and with a pool defined in the same stack; `ipv4CidrBlock` resolves to `Fn::GetAtt [<subnet>, CidrBlock]`; `PublicSubnet`/`PrivateSubnet` accept the prop (including `addNatGateway()`); a token `netmaskLength` is passed through; the three validation errors.
- New integration test `packages/@aws-cdk-testing/framework-integ/test/aws-ec2/test/integ.subnet-ipam.ts`: an IPAM pool provisioning the VPC's `10.0.0.0/16`, a `Subnet` with `ipv4IpamAllocation`, and an `awsApiCall('EC2', 'describeSubnets')` assertion that the allocated CIDR is `10.0.0.0/24`. I do not have an AWS account to deploy it, so the snapshot is not included; see the exemption request comment below.
- Build and checks run on GitHub Actions in my fork (same commit as this PR plus a fork-only workflow file): `yarn install`, `lerna run build --scope=aws-cdk-lib` (compile, eslint, awslint), `jest aws-ec2/test/vpc.test.ts` (157 tests), `yarn test aws-ec2`, and `yarn compat` all pass: https://github.com/gauranshahuja/aws-cdk/actions/runs/34515935447. A `jsii-rosetta extract --strict` run in the same workflow reports 52 diagnostics, all in pre-existing snippets of other modules' READMEs; the new `aws-ec2` README snippet produces none.

### Checklist
- [x] My code adheres to the [CONTRIBUTING GUIDE](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [DESIGN GUIDELINES](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md)

body:
## Summary

Closes #3803

Notes that mention a cashtag like `$BTC` can show a compact price card (price, 24h change, sparkline) below the note, similar to link previews.

- Cashtags are detected Swift-side from note content (`Cashtag.extract`), so nostrdb's block parser is untouched.
- Prices come from `https://ciphering.io/api/price/{SYMBOL}` via an actor with a 60s in-memory cache; concurrent requests for the same ticker share one fetch. All network work is off the main thread.
- On any network/decode error the card renders nothing, so notes are never affected.
- **Off by default.** Enabled under Appearance › Images › "Price cards for $tickers". No network request is made unless the user opts in.
- Respects `.no_previews` like link previews do.

## Checklist

- [x] I have read the Contribution Guidelines
- [x] I have tested the changes in this PR
- [x] I have profiled the changes to ensure there are no performance regressions, or I do not need to profile the changes.
    - If not needed, provide reason: feature is opt-in and off by default; the only added work per note is one regex scan of the content when enabled, and network fetches are cached and deduplicated.
- [x] I have filed or linked an existing issue/ticket related to this change (#3803)
- [x] My PR is either small, or I have split it into smaller logical commits
- [x] I have added the signoff line to all my commits
- [x] I have added appropriate changelog entries (`Changelog-Added`)
- [x] I have added appropriate `Closes:` tags in the commit messages

## Test report

**Device:** iPhone 17 Pro (Simulator)

**iOS:** _[fill in — Simulator › Settings › General › About]_

**Damus:** b90db082 (this branch, rebased on master 4a94f666)

**Setup:** Fresh account on the simulator. Price endpoint live at https://ciphering.io/api/price/BTC.

**Steps:**
1. Build and run; confirm timeline and notes render normally with the setting off (default) — no cards, no network calls.
2. Enable Appearance › Images › "Price cards for $tickers".
3. Post a note containing `$BTC`; open profile. Card appears under the note with price, 24h change and sparkline.
4. Post a note with `$BTC` and `$ETH`; two cards appear, deduplicated.
5. Post `$btc`, `$100`, `US$BTC`; no cards (covered by `CashtagTests`).
6. Turn the setting off; cards disappear on next render.
7. With the endpoint unreachable, notes render as if the feature were absent (skeleton briefly, then nothing).

**Results:**
- [x] PASS

## Other notes

`CashtagTests` covers extraction and boundary cases. The price source URL is a single constant (`CashtagPriceService.baseURL`) so it's easy to swap or make configurable if preferred. Happy to make the setting a Damus Labs experimental feature instead if that's the better fit.

author: mkhomutov
body:
## What

`component-architecture.md` now gives its arrows one meaning in both the Go and the Python group — an arrow follows a request, from the box that hands off part of the work to the box that does it — and the intro says so. The Go group gains the calls #904 left out (`server/` → `security/`, `observability/`, `registry/`; `channels/` → `wallet/`, `registry/`; `executor/` → `cost/`; `scheduler/` → `state/`) and turns the wrong `PLANNER --> SCHEDULER` arrow around. The Python group is redrawn along its request paths instead of class inheritance. Three real calls are listed in a new "Arrows left out" section rather than drawn. `system-overview.md` drops the same wrong planner arrow and draws the scheduler picking runs up from run state.

## Why

After #904 the intro said that Go arrows follow a request, but `security/` and `observability/` had none, and the channel router's calls to the wallet (`internal/channels/bounded_close.go`) and the registry (`grpc_dispatcher.go`) were left out. The Python group mixed three meanings: `BASE --> TASK` and `BASE --> PERSONA` were inheritance, while `PRUNTIME --> DISPATCH` pointed against both the import and the call (`agents/dispatch.py` and `agents/tick.py` import `persona_runtime`, not the reverse).

Checking every arrow against the code found more:

| Arrow | What the code does | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `PLANNER --> SCHEDULER` | Nothing calls the scheduler. `WorkflowScheduler.Run` polls `state/` every second for pending runs, re-parses the workflow with the planner and resolves each step's inputs (`planner.ResolveInputs`) | `SCHEDULER --> PLANNER` and `SCHEDULER -->\|pending runs\| STATE` |
| none | Every REST call passes the per-agent rate limiter (`security.RESTRateLimitMiddleware`) and security events go to the audit log; `persatrix logs` reads the log buffer; agents register over `POST /api/v1/agents/register` | `SERVER --> SEC`, `SERVER -->\|logs\| TELE`, `SERVER --> REGISTRY` |
| none | The router reads a conversation's spend from the wallet so it can close an autonomous channel's conversation before the budget runs out (RFC 0052 §D), and looks up each member agent's address | `CHAN -->\|conversation spend\| WALLET`, `CHAN --> REGISTRY` |
| none | The executor checks and fills the response cache for cacheable steps | `EXECUTOR -->\|response cache\| COST` |
| `Go <-.->\|gRPC\| Py` | Agents also call the REST API: they register at start, post channel messages and read channel history and members | label `gRPC · REST` |
| Python group | `ExecuteTask` reaches the agent's `handle` (a task agent runs the loop in `base.py`; a persona wraps the task as an event for its runtime); `ReceiveChannelMessage` goes through the event loop to `persona_runtime/`; `GetClosedInteractions` reads `memory/`; `SPAWN_SUB_AGENT` is answered `not_implemented` in `action_executor.py` | redrawn; the planned sub-agent arrow now leaves the dispatch box |

## How

- **One rule for Go and Python.** Arrows follow the hand-off of work, not imports: types, constants and logging, metrics and tracing helpers draw nothing, and neither does one class extending another. `task_agent.py → base.py` stays because a task agent runs the LLM and tool loop in `base.py`. In the Go group every hand-off is drawn except those listed.
- **Three calls listed, not drawn.** `scheduler/ → registry/` (each step's agent limits and model), `executor/ → security/` (one audit record per step) and `base.py → memory/` (only with `memory.enabled`). With every call drawn, the layouts tried had 10 to 24 crossings; each of these three caused several.
- **The layout is steered, and the source says so.** Invisible `~~~` links put `state/`, `planner/`, `executor/`, `registry/` and `cost/` on rows of their own and the loose stubs at the bottom, and the order of the arrows matters too; a `%%` comment in the block says both. One `~~~` in the overview keeps the scheduler beside run state.

## Not in this PR

- `workflow-execution.md` sequence 1 still shows the scheduler writing run state through the REST server, skips the polling hand-off, and says `202` where the handler answers `201`. That needs its own redraw on top of #922, which edits the same file.
- The README index row is unchanged: #922 rewrites the row next to it.

## Gates

`doc_links.py` ok (15 314 links, 567 files) · `file_size.py --strict` ok · `doc_status_markers.py` ok · `merged_prs.py --check` ok · pre-commit 12/12.

Mermaid, which CI does not render: both blocks parse and render in mermaid 11.4.1 and 10.9.1, and two deliberately broken copies fail in both. Measured on the rendered SVG, #904 → this PR (11.4.1 / 10.9.1):

| | Crossings | Edges through a box | Labels crossed by an edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| Component view | 3 → 1 / 2 → 1 | 0 → 0 / 0 → 0 | 0 → 0 / 1 → 0 |
| System overview | 14 → 14 / 41 → 42 | 4 → 4 / 7 → 6 | 2 → 2 / 2 → 2 |

The one crossing left in the component view is inside the Python group (`PRUNTIME --> LLM` over `BASE --> TOOLS`); the Go group has none. The overview's 11.4.1 layout is unchanged; on 10.9.1, 27 of its crossings come from the actor arrows in both versions. Every arrow starts at its source and ends, with its arrowhead, at its target (43 in the component view, 37 in the overview). Boxes and groups are unchanged (44 and 6; 27 and 4); component edges go from 34 to 43, the 7 dotted edges stay dotted, and all 7 stubs keep their dashed border.

## Review

Pending.

The `+` save-pin pill on the idle home sheet could never be enabled — `homeBottomCard()` only shows that sheet while `destination == null`, but the pill's `enabled` state required `destination != null`. author: tamnd
body:
Part of #58.

## Why this is the thing to do next

I triaged the forty three ClickBench queries against rudb this morning, as DuckDB writes them and with nothing rewritten, by building the `hits` schema from the official `create.sql` and putting each query through the binder and the executor. Thirty four of the forty three bind and run. The nine that do not are three causes: `EXTRACT(minute FROM EventTime)` in q19, `REGEXP_REPLACE` in q29, and comparing a `DATE` column against a string literal in q37 through q43.

So the SQL surface is not what stops rudb having an end to end number. What stops it is that there is no way to get the data in. `rudb-parquet`, `rudb-csv` and `rudb-arrow` were nine line stubs, and the only sources are `INSERT ... VALUES`, `range()` and `generate_series()`. That is why the 2a table has rudb abstaining on `clickbench` rather than losing.

The file we have to read is not a hard one. `hits_0.parquet` is SNAPPY, `PLAIN` plus `PLAIN_DICTIONARY` plus `RLE`, v1 pages, a million rows in two row groups. Snappy is a small decoder and dictionary pages land straight on the dictionary vector we already have, so the whole surface fits inside the zero dependency rule.

## What is in here

The footer, which is the half of a Parquet reader that decides how much of the file the other half has to touch.

`thrift.rs` is the compact protocol, written rather than depended on. It is a pull decoder: no derive, no intermediate tree, because a tree would allocate a node per field of a footer that on `hits` has a hundred and five columns in every row group, and every one of those nodes would be read once and dropped. An unknown field id is skipped by type, which is the property that keeps a reader written against one version of `parquet.thrift` working against a file written by a newer one.

`metadata.rs` is the structures: the schema, the row groups, and per column chunk the physical type, the codec, the encodings, where the pages start and what the writer said about the values. Three decisions worth naming:

- the bounds kept are `min_value` and `max_value` and not the deprecated `min` and `max`, because writers disagreed about how they ordered strings, which is why the newer fields exist, and a row group skipped on a bound whose ordering is in doubt is a wrong answer rather than a faster query
- a nested schema is an error naming the column it came from, because a repetition level this reader ignored would be a wrong answer and not a missing feature
- `logicalType` wins over `converted_type` where both are present, which matters on the one case where they disagree, a file whose `converted_type` says milliseconds and whose `logicalType` says nanoseconds

## Test gate

The fixture is 37 kilobytes written by DuckDB with Snappy, two row groups of 2048 rows, with one column of every shape the reader has to tell apart: plain and dictionary encoded, a column with nulls and columns without, a date and a timestamp. The tests check the schema against what DuckDB says the file is, that the row groups say where every column chunk is, that a dictionary column has a dictionary page and a plain one does not, and that the null count the writer wrote is the one in the data.

Every prefix of the footer parses as an error rather than a panic, and so does a footer longer than the file and a file that is not Parquet. Files from the other writers come in with the page decoders, since a writer's disagreements are about pages and not about the footer.

Gate is green on `server3`.

body:
## What this is

A singular `document.querySelector(...)` in a guard leg reads ONE element of a
population and the leg never says whether the population was 1, 3 or 40.
`view-scope-census.mjs` already classified every walk in `overflow-guard.mjs` by
SCOPE (document-wide vs live-view vs id-anchored). This adds the CARDINALITY
half, a register with a fatal staleness clause, a build-time CLI, and converts
six readiness gates to count the population they wait for.

## c0 — the build-time census, both reds proven

`node cloud/priv/static/__preview__/view-scope-census.mjs [--list]` — browserless,
dependency-free, wired as a new step in `console-unit` (`Singular-selector
population census (overflow-guard.mjs)`), placed so the derived-selection step at
the end of that job still picks up `view-scope-census.test.mjs` (its command line
is not a `node --test`, and the predicate strips comments before matching).

GREEN on this head:

```
SINGULAR-SELECTOR CENSUS — overflow-guard.mjs
  document.querySelector(All)? call sites: 272 (grep rule, for the header that used to type these: querySelector[(] 250 occurrences on 223 lines; querySelectorAll[(] 110 on 110)
  singular sites: 192
    counted-in-leg 20
    global-chrome  3
    live-view-host 61
    registered     85
    singleton-id   23
  register rows: 55
view-scope-census: every singular walk is accounted for, and every register row is reachable   (exit 0)
```

`--list` prints every singular site with its line, leg, selector and discharge.

Four classes are discharged BY RULE (an enumeration is a snapshot, a predicate is
a rule — 192 hand-kept rows would rot inside a wave): a terminal-`#id` selector,
the live-view host itself (`section.view:not([hidden])` — and NOT its
descendants, which are populations), page chrome from `GLOBAL_CHROME`, and a leg
that walks the SAME selector with `querySelectorAll` (i.e. prints the
population). Everything else owes a one-line reason in `SINGULAR_REGISTER`
(55 rows), keyed by leg + selector — never by line, because every line number in
this guard rots, which is exactly why the row this re-cuts was cancelled.

**RED ARM 1 — an unregistered singular walk.** Inserted
`void document.querySelector('.mutation-probe-row');` into the
GR115 leg:

```
  UNREGISTERED  GR115-bpconsole-dead-rule :: .mutation-probe-row (line 1996) — a singular walk with no printed population and no committed reason
view-scope-census: 1 unregistered singular walk(s), 0 stale register row(s). …
CONTROL A exit=1        (file restored → exit=0)
```

**RED ARM 2 — a register row nobody can reach (D180, staleness is fatal).** Added
one bogus row:

```
  STALE         GR115-bpconsole-dead-rule :: .deleted-walk — registered, but no singular walk in the guard matches it
view-scope-census: 0 unregistered singular walk(s), 1 stale register row(s). …
CONTROL B exit=1        (row removed → exit=0)
```

Both arms are also unit-tested over synthetic sources, each with its own control
(the same source with an empty register is clean on the stale arm), plus a
real-bytes arm asserting `unregistered == []` and `stale == []` against the
shipped guard.

### The stale header literals

`overflow-guard.mjs`'s header carried `68 occurrences / 55 lines / 15 All` as
hand-typed literals. Measured on `origin/main` the same three grep rules read
**253 / 224 / 98** (the filing said 97 for the third; `grep -o` and `grep -c` both
say 98). Every literal was dead by an order of magnitude, and the cancelled row
that sent somebody to look had quoted them. They are replaced by a pointer to the
census command, and `grepCounts()` now owns the derivation. A test reds if the
header types a count again — it was RED before the header edit and GREEN after.

## c1 — six readiness gates converted (D228), five populations provably > 1

Each converted gate counts the population it waits for and the leg PRINTS the
count. Where the element lives inside a view the count is scoped to
`section.view:not([hidden])` so it stays out of the document-wide residue class
W35 polices; the /new theater is its own page, so its gate is scoped to
`#new-body`.

| leg | selector | population measured |
|---|---|---|
| W12-narrow-viewport-truth | `.instances-grid .instance-card` | **5, 5, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2** (per scenario/theme) |

The last two are reported honestly: their populations are 1 on the shipped
fixture, so they are conversions, not >1 proofs. Five sites are provably >1.

BEFORE (origin/main, `.deploy-row`):

```
`document.querySelector('.deploy-row') && (function(){var v=document.querySelector('section.view:not([hidden])');return v && v.id==='view-site';})()`,
```

AFTER ok-lines, from a real browser run on this head:

```
✓ 12 / 12 cells clean across 320/390/620/900/1024/1440 in both themes — 12 cruel and 12 kind captions measured out of 24 .deploy-detail boxes, 0 page(s) dragging. The readiness gate stood in front of light:4 / dark:4 .deploy-row(s) in the visible view (D228: the gate counts the population it waits for, so a rail that painted ONE row of the fixture's list cannot pass for a rail that painted all of them). …
```

## Summary

Add real loopback protocol coverage for Vision Router's explicit proxy override without changing production behavior.

- exercise the actual Undici HTTP `ProxyAgent` path with a local CONNECT proxy and local HTTP target
- prove the HTTP proxy receives the unresolved provider host before tunneling the request
- exercise legacy `socks5h://` compatibility through Undici's SOCKS5 implementation
- prove the SOCKS proxy receives the unresolved domain name (`ATYP=0x03`) and the tunneled request reaches the target
- add bounded request timeouts plus forceful loopback socket cleanup so protocol regressions fail instead of hanging CI

## Why

H0/H1/H2 narrowed proxy ownership and retained explicit Vision Router HTTP/SOCKS overrides. Existing tests mostly verified dispatcher selection with fakes. This closes the remaining protocol-level evidence gap using real local proxy handshakes.

During development the first HTTP fixture expected absolute-form proxy requests and timed out. The investigation confirmed this was a test assumption bug: Undici 7.29 `ProxyAgent` defaults to `proxyTunnel=true`, so DVR correctly uses HTTP CONNECT. The final fixture validates the real protocol instead of changing production code.

## Validation

- `node --test --test-name-pattern='real loopback (HTTP proxy|SOCKS5)' tests/vision-provider-transport.test.js` → 2/2 pass
- `node --test tests/vision-provider-transport.test.js` → 23/23 pass

author: marcelveldt
body:
# What does this implement/fix?

A Sonos speaker playing a Music Assistant queue could start cutting out at a track change a
couple of tracks in, then fall silent, while Music Assistant kept showing it as playing.

A Sonos speaker reads its upcoming tracks from us in batches, and only asks for a new batch once
it has played through the one it holds. We were handing it just the playing track and the next
one, so two tracks in it ran out and had to fetch more right at the track change, which it fails.
It asks for up to ten, so that is what it now gets.

A track added to the queue while it plays still reaches it. When the speaker asks for a track it
cached before the change, that request is refused and it reads the queue again.

**Related issue (if applicable):**

- https://github.com/music-assistant/support/issues/6329

- Give a Sonos speaker as many upcoming tracks as it asks for, up to ten, instead of one.
- A track on repeat is still listed only once more, so switching repeat off takes effect after
  one more play, as before.
- A track the speaker was refused after a queue change is no longer logged as a failed track.
- Tests cover the deeper queue, repeat, a track added mid-playback, and refused tracks.

## Types of changes

- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) — `bugfix`
- [ ] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) — `new-feature`
- [ ] Enhancement to an existing feature — `enhancement`

- [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to not work as expected) — `breaking-change`

- [ ] Documentation only — `documentation`

- [ ] CI / workflow change — `ci`

## Checklist

- [x] `pytest` passes, and tests have been added/updated under `tests/` where applicable.

author: faridv
body:
## What

`npm run graph:check` — proves every cross-package import in every workspace package is an edge in the graph `nx affected` walks. Runs in `verify` and in CI, unconditionally, ahead of the affected step. Closes #49.

## Why

Consumer-fanout CI *works* (#304 touched `@atlas/messaging` and eight projects ran) but nothing guarded it. The two ways it breaks are silent — a relative import into another package, or an `@atlas/*` import the package never declared — and both compile, typecheck and pass tests. The package that lost its edge is then exactly the one `affected` skips. AGENTS.md §6 has warned about this in prose since the start.

## Proof the guard bites

| Planted defect | Result |
|---|---|
| `import ... from '../../data/src/db.ts'` in `@atlas/policy` | `✖ relative import escapes @atlas/policy into @atlas/data — import '@atlas/data' instead` |
| `import ... from '@atlas/messaging'` in `@atlas/policy`, undeclared | `✖ package.json does not declare it` **and** `✖ the Nx graph has no edge` |

Baseline: 15 packages, 30 edges, zero findings.

The second row is worth knowing: with `useInferencePlugins: false`, Nx builds this graph from `package.json` declarations, not from specifiers. "Declare it in package.json" is load-bearing, not tidy. AGENTS.md's trap row now says so.

## Adjacent, fixed in passing

`scripts/` has had an eslint block since the start and nothing ran it (not an Nx project → invisible to `nx affected -t lint`). Three real errors had accumulated. `npm run lint:scripts` now runs in CI and `verify`; the three are fixed — `URL` global, a dead initializer, and a thrown error that dropped `gh`'s real error instead of attaching it as `cause`.

## Not in scope

The local pre-push hook runs `nx run-many` only and doesn't run `api:check` either — left as is for parity.

author: paolovalletta-exelab
body:
## What changes

Two halves of one defect: some filenames produced an attachment that was stored and could never be opened.

**At the write.** `safeKeySegment` replaces a bare separator strip. Stripping `/` and `\` was not enough on its own: a name that *reduces* to `.` or `..` is a traversal the read side refuses, so it was written happily and then refused on every read. A file that exists and is unreachable forever is the worst of the three outcomes, which is why the rule belongs at the write — the key is what gets stored, and every later read is stuck with it.

Everything else is left alone, deliberately. A `#`, a `?` or a space is legal in a name and legal in a key; what they need is percent-encoding in the URL, not mangling at the write.

**At the read.** The panel interpolated the raw `s3Key` into the href in three places, so a filename carrying `#` was unreachable — everything after it became the fragment and never left the browser — and one carrying `?` landed as a query string. `attachmentHref` encodes each *segment*, never the key as a whole, since the slashes are the route's structure and must survive.

The `fileUpload` tool already built its display URL exactly this way (`s3Key.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/")`). This is the same rule on the reading side, which is where it was missing.

## How it was tested

- `npm run test:unit` — 252 files, 3064 passed, 3 skipped.
- `npm run typecheck` clean; `npm run lint` 0 errors (pre-existing warnings only).
- The new unit file pins both directions: what `safeKeySegment` refuses (a name reducing to a traversal, an empty or whitespace-only name) and what it must leave untouched (`report #12.pdf`, `report?.pdf`, `report..pdf`, `100%-done.pdf`).

## Related

polyant-ai/polyant#353 fixes the read side's own defect — the wildcard route param is an array of segments, not a string — and loosens the traversal check there to whole segments only, so `report..pdf` round-trips rather than being stored and refused. The two together are what make a filename with punctuation work end to end.

Not in this PR: attachment storage resolves secrets with `getAllSecrets`, so an organization-level `s3_bucket_name` is ignored. That is Enterprise-only — organization secrets do not exist here — and `config-resolver.ts` already carries the same divergence.
