author: astrapi69
body:
First, a correction to the issue's own premise, measured before building.

The issue says "**no test anywhere fires or simulates the idle timeout against a vault that is open
in the running application**". That was true when it was filed and is not true now. Three UI tests
merged since then drive the real `IdleLockWatchdog` against a real open vault over a moved clock:
`UnsavedWorkSurvivesTheIdleLockUiTest` (#304), `OpenEditorSurvivesTheIdleLockUiTest` (#303) and
`LockedVaultClosesItselfUiTest`.

What stayed true is the rest of it, and that is what this builds.

## The harness

`LockInvariantUiTest` enumerates `io.github.astrapi69.mystic.crypt.action` and asserts four
properties per action. The automatic lock cannot be brought into it: `IdleLockWatchdog` lives in the
`lock` package and is no `AbstractAction`, so the completeness check that catches a newly added
action never sees it.

`AutomaticLockHoldsTheInvariantUiTest` is the same shape with a different trigger. It opens a real
vault with a real entry, fires the real watchdog over a clock the test moves, and asserts the same
four:

- the workspace stays locked
- the vault is off screen
- the vault file is untouched
- nothing left on screen still shows the entry

Plus the fifth the invariant does not have, and this trigger needs: **nothing was lost.** An action
is something the user chose. The idle lock happens to somebody who walked away, so it may hide their
work and may not decide about it.

The three existing idle-lock tests each assert a slice of this for their own subject; none asserts
the invariant as an invariant, which is what the issue asked for.

## Two smaller things

The screen scan moved out of `LockInvariantUiTest` into `ScreenText` rather than being copied. It
walks labels, text components, tables and trees, and two copies of it drift the moment one learns
about a component type the other does not.

`LockInvariantUiTest`'s Javadoc names **both** of its boundaries now instead of one: plugin actions,
which are inline listeners in another module (#301), and code that acts on the lock without being an
action at all, which is this.

## Verification (local, and marked as local)

```
AutomaticLockHoldsTheInvariantUiTest + LockInvariantUiTest
  2 classes, 4 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped
```

Run under the #322 harness on a bare `Xvfb :99`. `LockInvariantUiTest` is in the run on purpose: it
is the class the scan was extracted from.

Closes #305

author: ahmedd-sherif
body:
Closes #12.

## What this does

Adds `validate_temporal_example`, one validator a producer calls with the
history it selected and the source events of that logical session, plus a
focused regression suite of known-good and deliberately leaking fixtures.

Checks, in the order the issue lists them:

- every history event is strictly before the decision, so a future target or
  outcome cannot reach the encoder;
- the T1 label is the first later different-item category, not an input;
- the T2 query is the item's first view and sits outside history, and a
  positive requires a later purchase of that item in the same session;
- no example, history row, target or outcome horizon crosses its approved
  temporal split, and an event exactly on the cutoff belongs only to the
  later split;
- an immature outcome stays censored with no label rather than becoming a
  negative;
- T3 timing is checked against the frozen protocol only.

## Why a validator rather than a re-implementation

The frozen notebooks persist decision metadata but not encoder-history rows,
and the real task example files carry `user_id`, so they are deliberately not
in this repository and cannot run in CI. Rebuilding examples here would create
a second builder to drift against. This validates what a producer already has.

The T3 gain rule is passed in by the caller and read in the tests from
`docs/evidence/s1-d1-ds-07/t3_protocol_v1.proposed.json`, so this module cannot
introduce a competing gain mapping. The same-category eligibility it asserts is
read back from `docs/evidence/s1-ds-09/g1_gate_v1.frozen.json`.

## Validation

- `ruff check ppsi scripts tests` passes.
- `python -m pytest -q` passes: 584 tests.
- `python -m pytest -q tests/test_temporal_leakage.py` passes: 10 tests, and the
  known-good case is validated twice in one run to show it is deterministic.
- Each deliberate leak fails on its own named invariant, not a generic error.

Runs through the existing CI workflow from #22; no new workflow is added.

author: shomix
body:
Beta and production now migrate the database independently, so a new column must never be added in a way that breaks existing data or already-running code.

## Summary

Our rule has always been that database changes must be additive: never drop, rename, or destructively change a table or column. 

A new column could still be added as required (`NOT NULL`) without saying what value it should get for rows that already exist. That breaks the moment it runs, and it also breaks any already-deployed code that inserts rows without knowing the new column exists.

body: Rebuild `/how-it-works` to match the Home and Business Profile Recovery conversion standard, without changing any other page. ## What changed The page now answers “If I contact ReputeDefend, what actually happens?” with a shorter, customer-facing structure: 1. Hero — existing H1 kept: “A clear process for situations that rarely feel clear.” 2. Service trust strip 3. Four-step primary journey 4. What to send / start with what you have 5. Four assessment lenses 6. What you can expect back 7. Two equal service paths 8. Positive trust / transparency (one platform-limitation callout) 9. Six FAQs 10. Dark final conversion Primary CTA is **Tell us what happened** → `/get-help`. Submitting an enquiry is framed as a human review, not a paid commitment. ## What was consolidated - Six-step railway journey → four customer-facing steps, including **You decide how to proceed** - Removed standalone **What we do not do** (`HowLimits`) and **Communication** (`HowCommunication`) - Useful limitation and communication ideas merged into one light trust section plus a single Google-controls-outcomes callout - FAQs reduced from 10 to 6, including paid-commitment and account-access reassurance - “What to send” reduced to six optional items with a password/credential safety callout ## Structured data `HowToStructuredData` uses the same four `journeySteps` shown on the page: 1. author: soudjaymoursala-netizen
body:
## Contexte

Suite de #27 (mergée) : la migration Dexie v33 supprime la table locale `normativeDocuments` (Bibliothèque de normes) sans jamais sauvegarder son contenu au préalable. Un navigateur ayant importé des documents avant le passage au stockage serveur (R2+D1) les aurait perdus **définitivement** dès la première ouverture avec ce code — risque identifié après le merge de #27, avant que l'utilisateur ne rouvre l'outil sur l'ordinateur où ces documents avaient été importés.

## Changement

- `persistance/db.ts` : la montée de version 33 capture désormais le contenu de l'ancienne table `normativeDocuments` (via `tx.table(...).toArray()`, encore accessible pendant la transaction d'`upgrade()`, avant la suppression physique) dans `documentsNormatifsAMigrer` — vide sur un navigateur déjà passé par cette version.
- `useNormativeDocumentsStore.ts` : `migrerDocumentsLocauxVersServeur()`, appelée au début de `charger()`, envoie chaque document capturé au serveur (même chemin que l'import direct) puis le retire de la file — retiré uniquement après succès, pour réessayer automatiquement au prochain chargement en cas d'échec réseau.
- Tests : `db.migration.test.ts` (capture réelle via une base IndexedDB seedée à l'ancien schéma, contenu binaire inclus ; non-régression si la table est déjà absente) + 2 tests dans `useNormativeDocumentsStore.test.ts`.

## Validation

- `npx vitest run` (repo racine) : 1118/1118 passés.
- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint` : OK.

body:
New work must remain independently reviewable, even when earlier work is still awaiting merge. Every new feature, independent fix, cleanup or documentation change now starts on a fresh branch based on the preceding work branch, with its PR targeting that parent.

Document this in the repository-level AGENTS.md and bilingual workflow, including parent-first merging, child PR retargeting before branch deletion, and a prerelease version per PR. Same-feature review corrections can remain on their branch. Existing PR history is not rearranged.

Stack: this PR targets feature/deploy-mobile and follows #9. Its diff contains only the workflow agreement and required version/changelog update.

Validation: all 3 version tests passed, including the runtime version endpoint; git diff --check passed. No paid model calls or local Docker startup.

author: jfolcini
body:
Closes #4958

Clear a parent block's text and press Backspace once more: the whole outline under it vanished. The keymap's Backspace-on-empty rule reads `editor.isEmpty`, which sees only this block's own text, so a blank parent routed to `handleDeleteBlock`, whose `remove` is a backend cascade soft-delete. When the parent was collapsed nothing on screen hinted the keystroke would touch more than one row.

**Shape: re-parent, matching the merge path** (the issue's preferred option). `handleDeleteBlock` now calls the same `planChildReparent(blocks, focusedBlockId, prevBlock.id)` the merge handlers call for #1342 and chains `moveBlocks(...).then(() => remove(...))`, preserving the move-before-remove ordering `mergeBlocksAndHandle` enforces. Planned from the full flat tree, since the collapsed projection hides exactly the children at stake. The merge handlers' revert-the-edit / remount machinery was not lifted: a delete has no edit to revert. With no previous visible block to adopt the children (first row), the delete does not proceed, mirroring the merge handlers' `idx <= 0` bail and Guard 3 in `empty-block-cleanup.ts`. Childless deletes are unchanged. `prevBlock` is computed once and reused by the existing post-delete focus branch.

One thing worth knowing: the store's `moveBlocks` swallows its own errors, but `BlockTree.tsx` hands the hook a wrapper that re-reads the tree and throws when a child did not land under the new parent, so the `.then` chain really does skip the `remove` on a failed reparent. A test pins that.

**Tests** (five new cases in the `handleDeleteBlock` describe, asserting on re-queried `parent_id` state through a store model whose `remove` takes the same transitive closure the backend cascade takes): collapsed blank parent → parent removed, both hidden children under the previous sibling; expanded variant; first-row blank parent → nothing removed; childless delete → no `moveBlocks`; failed reparent → `remove` skipped. Red on a copy with the pre-`remove` block reverted: `expected [ 'A' ] to deeply equal [ 'A', 'B1', 'B2' ]` (the store lost the parent and both hidden children); the failed-reparent case separately: `expected [ 'A' ] to deeply equal [ 'A', 'B', 'B1', 'B2' ]`. The 109 pre-existing cases (last-block guard, #4552 list-style step-down, #1342 merge reparenting) stay green in both directions.

`docs/FEATURE-MAP.md` untouched: it documents no Backspace behaviour.

Verified: orchestration file 114 passed; `BlockTree`, `use-block-keyboard`, enter-split-race 363 passed; `npm run typecheck` exit 0. Session log 1701.

author: pblumer
body:
Closes #886.

[ADR-0259](docs/adr/0259-data-object-lifecycle.md) gave a class a state machine, and it was written against a real model that already had one — drawn as an enumeration.

That model is the whole problem statement. Its author had written the five states of an identity as literals of an «enumeration», with a paragraph of documentation on each, *because that was the only place the states could be written down at all*. ADR-0259 then added a second place, and the model said the same five strings twice: once as literals a person maintained, once as states a deploy resolved against. Nothing connected them, nothing noticed when they drifted, and the documentation — the half worth more than the strings — sat on the half the engine does not read.

## What it does

`Lifecycle.StatesFrom` names an «enumeration» in the same model, and that enumeration's literals **are** the states. The name of a state is written in one place. Everything an enumeration cannot hold stays on the lifecycle, which is most of what a lifecycle is for: which state instances are created in, which end the life, what may follow what, and where each sits on the canvas.

The two statements stay apart, and that is the point. The enumeration answers *which values are there*; the lifecycle answers *in what order*. Neither is derivable from the other, so this is a reference between them rather than a merge of them.

| Gesture | What happens |
|---|---|
| Rename a literal | The state is renamed, and every transition naming it is rewritten |
| Remove a literal | The state goes, and the arrows touching it go with it |
| Add a state on the sheet | The literal is written, because that is where the names live |
| Unhook the enumeration | The states stay — they were this class's states all along |
| Rename the enumeration | The reference follows the name |

Renaming a literal renaming the state is not a new rule: it is what renaming a state already does, because a state's name **is** the string every process writes. Adding a state writing the literal is the same reasoning from the other end — a state the enumeration does not declare is one the server refuses, and a palette that draws something unsaveable is a trap.

On a sourced lifecycle the state's name is shown **read-only** and says where it is renamed. Hiding the field or silently dropping the edit would both be worse surprises.

## The tie, in the class diagram

A dashed `«lifecycle»` dependency from the class to the enumeration, derived from the reference and never authored. It is the store link's construction ([ADR-0230](docs/adr/0230-process-information-model.md) §7) pointed at a different pair, for that construction's reason: a class and an enumeration do not *relate*, one *takes its states from* the other.

So `AllowAssociation` is untouched, an enumeration is still not the end of a relationship, and nothing that counts relationships counts this line. The keyword is the notation — UML allows many dependencies and draws them all as one dashed line, so `«lifecycle»` is what says which one this is.

The bundle grew 367 bytes (161,287 → 161,654), which is the renderer arithmetic rather than the library's: an open arrowhead, a keyword, and one more derived edge in the reconcile.

## What is refused, and what deliberately is not

Three refusals, all the same kind — the document claims its states come from a set and then contradicts itself about what that set is or what is in it:

- `lifecycle-unknown-enumeration` — the reference names no class in the model
- `lifecycle-not-an-enumeration` — it names something that is not one
- `state-not-a-literal` — a state the enumeration does not declare, reported **on the state** so the canvas marks it

A literal with **no** state is not refused. A machine half drawn is the normal condition every rule in that validator is careful about, and "you declared a value you have not placed yet" is incompleteness rather than incoherence.

A lifecycle that names no enumeration behaves exactly as it did before this existed.

## Verification

```
go build ./...                     ok
go vet ./...                       clean
gofmt -l .                         empty
go test -race -timeout=25m ./...   68 packages ok
e2e (Playwright)                   974 passed
```

`validateLifecycle` is at 100% statement coverage. Eight new e2e tests cover the drawing and every gesture above; three break-tests confirm they hold something — dropping the literal-rename, emptying the machine on unhook, and drawing the tie without its keyword each fail exactly one test.

Two failures in an earlier run were chased down rather than waved past. `TestKeyFeaturesTileIsReviewedAgainstTheChangelog` was real: it makes every new Added bullet ask whether the Console's "what Atlas is" tile is still complete. The answer here is no, nothing to add — "Data with a model behind it" covers it — so the marker moved, which is the normal outcome that check exists to force. `TestRestartDuringBackoffTriesAgainImmediately` is timing-sensitive and was running against a machine busy with the Playwright suite; alone under `-race` it passes repeatedly, and the final full run is green with nothing else loading the machine.

The ADR arrives with its code, so it reads `Accepted` / `Landed`. It is still a draft — no number, no index row — and `make adr-number` assigns one when it lands on main.

body:
## Summary

- The weekly `vulnerability-scan.yml` workflow always created a fresh timestamped branch/PR on every run, with no check for a still-open PR from a previous run, letting duplicate `fix: resolve vulnerabilities detected by govulncheck` PRs pile up unmerged.
- Closed the 12 stale duplicates (#27-#38) that had accumulated since 2026-06-15.

author: elijah-ezaga
body:
teamscale-upload 3.0.0 makes every upload an explicit command, so the action has to name one. Add a `command` input that selects between `report` and `vulnerability-report`. It defaults to `report`, so existing workflows keep working unchanged.

`vulnerability-report` needs a build name and version, so add the `build-name` and `build-version` inputs. They are declared optional in action.yml, because an input required by one command is unused by the other, and the script checks per command that the ones it needs are there. Inputs belonging to the other command are simply not passed on.

Bump the pinned teamscale-upload to v3.0.0. The version was set in the environment but never read, since the script hardcoded the download URL, so wire it up and fail the download on an HTTP error instead of unpacking the error page.

author: agoscinski
body:
This adds restarts the tests for each test requiring the daemon. In principle it is not needed, if we would don't have side effects on session scoped fixtures in the tests but we have them and it is hard to detect them and fix all of them. The disadvantage is that this increases our testing time a bit because of the daemon restarts but it is not significant.  The time we loose to fix or restart flaky tests is much worse. Also an xfail is added in case the daemon is not reachable because for example the GitHub runners are overloaded again. There I added the logic to actually force kill the daemon if one stop the daemon regularly to avoid that an xfail leaves a unbound daemon process open when continuing running other tests.

There as an additional fix (third commit) that is not directly a test that is related to the daemon, but makes tests fail that start a daemon and keep it open fail because they change the session profile which is not registered when the daemon is started. Therefore these tests are changed to a function-scoped profile. With the preceding changes this should not happen anymore because the daemon would have been restarted between tests but in general it is good habit to scope tests correctly (if they change a resource of a session scope fixture and dont change it back, then they should use a function scoped fixture).

author: buzzdan
body:
## Summary

Companion to [buzzdan/ai-coding-rules#30](https://github.com/buzzdan/ai-coding-rules/pull/30), which gives `/go-ldd-review` a scope ladder that never widens on its own: an argument (`--all` for the whole repository), else the working tree's changes, else the current branch against its base, else "nothing to review".

On the clean single-commit fixture the bare command therefore has nothing to review. That flips the reading of baseline finding 1: the two `review-full` runs that reported an empty scope were correct, and the one that audited the repository unasked was the defect.

- **`review-full`** now invokes `/go-ldd-review --all`, so the case measures whole-repository recall again instead of scope guessing. Graders unchanged.
- **`review-clean-tree`** (new, cheap, 3 runs, about $0.15 each) runs the bare command and expects: "nothing to review" in the report, the `--all` form named, no `Agent` spawned (`tool_used` max 0), and no cluster entry or per-rule finding tally.
- **Baseline README**: an errata paragraph under finding 1 records the decided contract and says the recorded verdicts stand; future `review-full` runs compare against run 1's 90 of 111.

Validated against the #30 plugin checkout: `review-clean-tree` 3/3, $0.45. One report, verbatim: "Scope: Rung 4 — nothing to review. Working tree is clean, `master` has a single commit, and there are no remotes or other branches to diff against … No hunter/skeptic review was run (no verdict over an empty scope). For a whole-repository audit, re-run with `--all`."

`task go:manifest` passes; the generated review-full graders are unchanged.

Merge after #30, since `review-full --all` and the control both assume the ladder.

author: yameenbux
body:
Measured before touching anything: **1358px at 1440 for a carousel 599px high**. 380 of that was section padding, 246 the heading block, and 76 the Instagram line sitting under the carousel with a gap above it.

## The carousel is not touched

It was sized once, resized on request, then put back where it started — that is settled, and shaving it again to win pixels would be relitigating a decision already made. Cards measure 400px at 1440 and 225px on a phone, exactly as before.

## Three things changed instead

**The heading lost its line break.** "The portfolio" on one line rather than two, at the same size on the same scale — no type change, **99px saved**, and one decisive line reads sharper against a strip of photographs than a stacked pair. The other headings keep their breaks; this one is short enough not to need one, and wraps by itself on a phone.

**The band opts down** to `clamp(72px, 12vh, 128px)`, the same figure `#maintenance` now takes. The site-wide `--band` is untouched.

**The Instagram line moved onto the heading row**, where the right half was empty anyway. Done with named grid areas rather than source order, so the markup still reads heading → work → elsewhere, which is the order it should be read and heard in. Below 720px the areas restack and it returns to underneath the work — you do not point somebody elsewhere before you have shown them anything.

Also trimmed `.cf-caption`'s reserved box from `3.2em` to `2.6em`. It is there so the dots do not jump between captions of different lengths, and none of hers needs that much.

author: cacack
body:
Clears the last open Dependabot alert on the repo ([#13](https://github.com/cacack/waterforge/security/dependabot/13), high, CVSS 5.9, CVE-2026-67213). The other 19 alerts are already fixed.

## The advisory

nanoid before 3.3.18 loops forever in `customAlphabet` and `customRandom` when either is called with a `size` of 0 — the generation loop never satisfies its exit condition and hangs the calling thread.

## Why the practical exposure here is nil

Two independent reasons, both worth recording so the next person doesn't re-derive them:

1. **The vulnerable functions are never called.** nanoid is reached only as `vite@8.0.16 → postcss@8.5.23 → nanoid`. postcss's sole use is `lib/input.js`, which does `require('nanoid/non-secure')` and calls `nanoid(6)` — the plain generator, with a hardcoded size. Neither `customAlphabet` nor `customRandom` is involved.
2. **It never reaches users.** nanoid runs during the CSS build. `grep -rl nanoid dist/` returns nothing.

Dependabot labels the scope "runtime" only because `vite` sits in `dependencies` under this repo's dist-based split convention. In fact it is build-time.

## The change

postcss's range is `^3.3.11`, so `npm update nanoid --package-lock-only` resolves it with no manifest change and no other package touched — 3 lines of `package-lock.json`.

## On the commit type

`.github/dependabot.yml` prefixes `dependencies`-side bumps with `fix`, which would cut a patch release. Since nothing in `dist/` changes, that release would deliver nothing to users, so this is typed `chore` — the alert clears in the lockfile without a release. Flagging it explicitly since it departs from what the Dependabot config would have produced.

## Verification

All four checks green on this branch after `npm ci`:

- `npm run lint` — eslint, prettier, shadcn data-attr check
- `npm run typecheck` — svelte-check 4565 files, 0 errors; tsc
- `npm run test` — 254 tests, 16 files
- `npm run build` — clean, PWA precache 30 entries

## Side note, not addressed here

Before this branch, `node_modules` was stale — `svelte-eslint-parser@1.8.0 invalid: "^1.8.1" from the root project`. The `npm ci` run for this PR resolved it locally, but that was a local-checkout drift, not a repo change.

author: crossbizz
body:
## Summary

Add bounded, enrollment-bound producer generations and consumer slots with durable chunk checkpoints, acknowledgment, crash recovery, reclamation and retirement. Install separate producer/consumer roles and strict owned/projected token readers. Add schema 48 and real API acceptance receipts for exact replay across credential rotation without duplicate work. Keep frontend enrollment binding and generated API contracts aligned.

The final security review found that producer drops and interrupted counter uncertainty could disappear from health after reclamation. The fix persists identity-bound, bounded coverage accounting before acknowledgment and retirement. Retries and slot reuse don't double-count, missing history degrades coverage, and damaged accounting blocks acknowledgment.

CI now exposes all required PostgreSQL fixture executables before verification and runs sensor lineage and authenticated replay tests. The composed harness SIGTERM test uses an owned private temporary directory and guaranteed child cleanup.

Hosted CI then found that interrupting `go build` could leave its compiler descendants running. The correction gives commands isolated POSIX process groups, bounded TERM/KILL, waits for inherited output pipes to close, and keeps compiler scratch under the owned harness root. Four deterministic helper regressions and cold-cache harness interruption pass; review found no remaining blocker. The final composed browser/API/worker rerun passed and completed every owned cleanup phase. That correction's push and PR checks passed cleanup but failed released migration 13 on PostgreSQL 16.15. Later sensor/Attack Lab stages were skipped, not passed. Exact run IDs are recorded in the release verification document.

Disposable PostgreSQL 16.12 reproduces the migration refusal. Exact catalog comparison against local 18.3 found 135 extra NOT NULL catalog records and 18 MAINTAIN table ACL entries on 18, changing the pinned fingerprint. Released SQL and drift-denial checks are unchanged. CI now selects an explicit PostgreSQL 18 reference major on Ubuntu 24.04 through the signed PGDG repository with a hash-checked key and actual server-major check. This is not a repair of older-major compatibility or an 18-only product contract. Original Neon/SaaS/single-tenant scope remains intact; supported majors and a reachable bootstrap/upgrade compatibility path remain open production gates. Current-head CI must pass before merge.

## Verification

- Full platform race suite: 79 packages passed with serial package scheduling.
- Final sensor race suite: passed in 120.511 seconds. Adapter compatibility races passed.
- Full UI verification: 1,180 tests, typecheck, lint, contracts, production build, compiled imports and 728-row ledger passed.
- Final ordinary Linux binary: UID/GID65532, no capabilities/network, 217 top-level passes and 20 explicit fixture-only skips.
- Actual non-root executable: three owned-file upload/cleanup lifecycles passed, including token removal before cleanup.
- Local composed Chrome/runtime-worker proof and release-source gate passed. Browser console was clean and owned cleanup completed.
- Independent review found no remaining concrete blocker in the final loss-accounting or SIGTERM changes.
- Cleanup correction: fresh full UI/build and source-release gates passed; all 71 selected Node CI tests passed (two explicit opt-in signal fixtures skipped). The final composed runtime/browser run exited 0 with a clean browser console and complete owned cleanup, recorded in `/tmp/zasp-lineage-process-group-composed.log`.
- Reference database correction: 19 workflow tests and the dependent release contract pass after RED regressions; independent re-review reports no remaining concrete finding. Fresh full verification passes 1,184 UI tests, typecheck/lint, contracts, production build and the unchanged ledger. Both new hosted runs installed the reference packages and passed UI/build, cleanup, release-source and maintenance alerts; complete current-head CI remains pending.
- Isolated non-root Linux PostgreSQL 18.6 matches the pinned v13 fingerprint and passes actual empty-to-48, idempotency, rollback, v1-to-48 and checksum-drift refusal in 6.02 seconds. This is not older-major compatibility or deployed acceptance proof.

Both reference-environment CI runs later passed the actual migration suite but failed the paired sensor-create test with HTTP 503. The handler compared its nanosecond expiry with PostgreSQL's microsecond value after committing the token. A forced-clock PostgreSQL test reproduced the defect. The correction canonicalizes intended expiry before mutation and preserves exact returned credential authority checks. Fifty create/rotate precision cases reject positive and negative expiry drift; real create/rotate/readback/replacement-token ingest and revoked-token denial pass in focused host races and non-root Linux PostgreSQL 18.6. Independent review reports no findings. Fresh full UI/build and release-source gates pass. The first full API invocation predates a new test's corrected 401-to-403 expectation and isn't final passing evidence; final-code full API verification and fresh hosted checks remain required before merge.

author: devfirmino
body:
Second section of the series, matching [blog post part 2](https://github.com/DeVFirmino/danielsite/pull/139).

## Contents

- `README.md` — the verb/type/name shape, `run` vs `create`, labels, `expose`, Service types and ports, and where one command stops being enough
- `pod-with-label.yaml`, `pod-and-service.yaml`, `deployment.yaml`, `service-nodeport.yaml` — real `--dry-run` output

## Two things worth noting

**The generated YAML is genuine output, and getting it exposed a fact worth documenting.** `kubectl run --dry-run=client` contacts the API server for discovery and fails without a reachable cluster, so `pod-with-label.yaml` and `pod-and-service.yaml` needed the kind cluster. `create service` and `create deployment` generate offline. The README states this, because "client dry-run means no cluster contact" is a common and wrong assumption.

**`run` and `create deployment` label pods differently**, which decides whether `create service` finds them:

| Command | Label on the pods |
|---|---|
| `kubectl create deployment web` | `app: web` |
| `kubectl run httpd` | `run: httpd` |

Since `create service NAME` defaults to the selector `app: NAME`, it matches the deployment's pods and misses the `run` pod.

Also removes the `kubectrl` typo bullet from section 01: it was an accidental keystroke, not a real trap.

Verified on a throwaway kind cluster (v1.37.0), including the NodePort range rejection and the `all` category membership.

author: peterettwein-evelix
body:
﻿## Problem

Bei der Synchronisation einer VE mit Primärdaten blieben Ordner im Verzeichnis `@@CMI.Manager.DocumentConverter.Properties.DocumentConverterSettings.BaseDirectory@@` (`ConverterBaseFolder\<JobGuid>`) samt Inhalt liegen, obwohl die Synchronisation erfolgreich durchlief. In den Logs war kein Fehler zu finden.

## Ursache

Der `JobEndRequest` — der einzige Auslöser für das Löschen des Jobordners und des SFTP-Users — wurde in `TextEngine.ExtractText` und `RenderEngine.ConvertFile` nur im Erfolgspfad gesendet.

Ist ABBYY nicht installiert (`PathToAbbyyFrEngineDll` leer), liefert `AbbyyTextExtractor` nur eine **Warning** `Path to FrEngine.dll not set` und ein Ergebnis mit `HasError = true`. `TextEngine` fängt das ab und kehrt mit `return string.Empty;` zurück — **vor** dem `JobEndRequest`. Ergebnis: Sync läuft „erfolgreich" durch, kein Error im Log, aber Jobordner und SFTP-User bleiben dauerhaft liegen. Dasselbe gilt für alle Exception-Pfade in beiden Engines.

Zusätzlich brach das Cleanup in `SftpServer.RemoveJobInternal` still ab, wenn der SFTP-User bereits entfernt war (`user == null` → `return`), sodass auch ein später doch noch eintreffender `JobEndRequest` den Ordner nicht mehr löschen konnte.

## Änderungen

- **`CMI/Engine/Asset/TextEngine.cs`** — `JobEndRequest` in einen `finally`-Block verschoben und die `JobGuid` aus dem `JobInitResult` verwendet statt aus dem Extraction-Result (das bei `IsInvalid` nicht befüllt wird). Fehler beim Aufräumen werden nur als Warning geloggt, damit sie den ursprünglichen Fehler nicht überdecken.
- **`CMI/Engine/Asset/RenderEngine.cs`** — dieselbe Korrektur für `ConvertFile`.
- **`CMI/Manager/DocumentConverter/SftpServer.cs`** — `RemoveJob` räumt Verzeichnis, JobInfo und SFTP-User jetzt unabhängig voneinander auf. `GetJobInfo` liefert `null` statt einer `KeyNotFoundException`; die Consumer prüften bereits auf `null`.

## Test

- `CMI.Manager.DocumentConverter`, `CMI.Engine.Asset` und `CMI.Manager.DocumentConverter.Tests` bauen fehlerfrei im Release
- 9/9 DocumentConverter-Tests grün
- Fachlich zu prüfen: Nach einer Synchronisation einer VE mit Primärdaten auf einem System ohne ABBYY-Installation darf im `BaseDirectory` kein Jobordner zurückbleiben.

## Deploymentrelevante Punkte

Keine. Bereits liegengebliebene Ordner im `ConverterBaseFolder` müssen einmalig manuell entfernt werden.

author: hassnalalshaikh
body:
fix(core): provide observation helpers to workflow tools

## Problem

A declarative workflow whose step is a tool entry (`runToolEntry`) calls the tool's `execute` without the observation helpers that `Agent`-invoked tools receive. A tool that uses `context.observe` (or the related helpers) crashes inside a workflow with `observe is not a function`, while the same tool works when the agent calls it directly.

## Fix

`packages/core/src/workflows/entry-executors/run-tool-entry.ts` now passes the same observation helpers into the tool execution context that the agent tool path provides, so a tool behaves identically whether an agent or a workflow step runs it.

## Test

`packages/core/src/workflows/entry-executors/run-tool-entry.test.ts` runs a tool entry that calls the observation helpers and asserts the step completes with the tool's output instead of throwing.

Changeset: patch for `@mastra/core` (and the packages that re-export the workflow runtime).

Branch: `hassnalalshaikh:fix/workflow-tool-observation-helpers` (one commit on current `main`).

author: bahaa37
body:
The site claimed solution architect in its title, hero and meta description while every
entry in the experience record said Senior Full-Stack Software Engineer, over a career
starting March 2023. A reader screening for that title finds the contradiction on the
same page and stops, so the claim was costing the screen it was meant to win.

Reposition on what the record shows — a senior .NET engineer working at architecture
level — and let the DTC removal and the payment middleware make the architecture
argument on their own. The architecture vocabulary stays; the unsupported job title
does not.

Alongside that:

- Split the summary in two. The showcase page gets ~70 words, because the top of a CV
  competes with the back button; the printed CV keeps the long version, which is what
  an ATS indexes and what someone who already opened the PDF is willing to read.
- Regroup skills from ten flat categories into seven ranked ones. jQuery, Ajax, HTML5,
  CSS3, plain JavaScript, OOP and TFS are dropped: on an architecture CV they cost more
  in dilution than they earn. .NET Framework, .NET Core and ASP.NET MVC move under
  Legacy Modernization, where they read as the systems being modernized rather than as
  the current toolkit. Integration keywords keep a group of their own because /cv is
  parsed by software that matches on exactly those terms.
- Add timezone, notice, relocation and languages. These are what a recruiter asks in
  their first reply in all three target markets, and for a remote or relocation role
  they are often what decides whether the reply comes at all.
- State the career change into software engineering rather than leaving 2019-2022 as a
  gap the reader fills in unfavourably.
- Reorder the Windoor write-up's account of the 72 red tests so the reason arrives
  before the number. The explanation was already there; a skimming reviewer met "72
  tests failed" first and did not reach it.

Guard all of it in RealCvDocumentTests, which already asserts against the live cv.json:
summary length, the long summary's presence, the recruiter fields, the group cap, and
no skill duplicated across groups. The last of those caught Blazor listed twice.

Add ci.yml so the tests run on branches and pull requests. They previously ran only on
a push to main, which meant a broken build was found during a deploy, with the bad
commit already on the default branch.

author: antsok
body:
## Summary

`Docker (live)` has been red since #1091 merged. The live Bicep confinement probe builds its router without a cleanup floor, so it now resolves `Cleanup.DISPOSE` and fails its first assertion before measuring anything. It opts into `Cleanup.RECLAIM`, the way sample 13 already does.

## Related issue

Fixes #1110. Tracked by #1107.

## Changes

- `packages/maf-sandbox-bicep/tests/test_bicep_confinement_e2e.py`: pass `min_cleanup=Cleanup.RECLAIM` when constructing the router.

## Stacked on #1111

This branch carries #1111's commit because the pre-push hook refuses any branch from a Windows checkout until it lands — `main` does not type-check there. Merge #1111 first and this diff reduces to the one file above. Nothing here depends on it otherwise.

## Why this and not a weaker assertion

#1091 made cleanup resolve from backend capabilities and floors alone — `established_cleanup` no longer reads the spec, and `confined_to_guest_call_path` reaches neither `_router.py` nor `_cleanup.py`. That is deliberate and already documented: `packages/maf-sandbox-bicep/README.md` calls the metadata advisory with core 0.38, and `docs/sandbox/kinds/bicep.md` records warm validation as something a host opts into. So the default is right and the test was encoding the old one.

Relaxing the expectation to `DISPOSE` would have deleted the coverage rather than repaired it. The probe measures that a call leaves nothing behind **and** returns the same `instance_id` twice over; under disposal there is no instance left to measure, and the row in `docs/sandbox/kinds/bicep.md` claiming "the Docker probe measures successful validation, diagnostics, module restores and cancellation twice on the same instance" would become false on purpose.

#1091 updated every offline sibling of this assertion — `test_cleanup_resolution.py`, `test_cleanup_ladder.py`, `test_sandbox_router.py`, `test_bicep_workload.py` — and opted sample 13 in. This file and `test_bicep_cache_e2e.py` are the two that run only in `docker-live.yml`, and were missed. `test_bicep_cache_e2e.py` builds no router and needed no change; this was the last site in the repository reading the router default.

## Verification

Both directions measured locally against a real Docker engine, with `bicep-sandbox:ci` built from `images/bicep-sandbox` and the pinned observer image:

- [x] With the fix: `5 passed in 168.94s` — all five cases, `modules` included, with `MAF_SANDBOX_DOCKER_E2E_PROXY_IMAGE` set so the AVM restore runs rather than skipping.
- [x] Reverted as a control: `test_..._reuses_the_sandbox[local]` fails with `AssertionError: assert <Cleanup.DISPOSE: 'dispose'> is <Cleanup.RECLAIM: 'reclaim'>`, identical to the three CI runs.
- [x] `uv run poe doc-trackers`: 236 rows checked.
- [x] Full local `uv run poe gate`: 7,449 passed, 232 skipped, **2 failed** — both pre-existing on unmodified `main` at `2e63fd9e` and unrelated to this change, detailed below.

## Two gate failures that are not this change

Reproduced on a detached checkout of `origin/main` with nothing applied:

- `tests/test_workflow_selection.py::test_workflow_marker_discovers_a_new_module` — asserts `b"1 passed, 1 deselected"` against subprocess output that arrives carrying ANSI escapes under `pwsh`, so the plain bytes never match. From the Windows workflow tooling in #1073.
- `packages/maf-sandbox/tests/test_host_tools_over_exec.py::TestTheLauncherAgainstARealShell::test_a_program_that_prints_and_then_hangs_leaves_its_output_readable` — "the launcher never created the output file". From the launcher rewrite in #1091.

Both are Windows-local; Linux CI is green on them. Left alone rather than folded in here.

## Not covered, deliberately

Bicep's **new** default — disposal after every call — is exercised by no live test. It is not a parametrisation of this one: `assert_nothing_left_behind` adopts an instance and fingerprints it either side of the call, which assumes the instance survives. Under `DISPOSE` there is nothing left to fingerprint, so covering it needs a different measurement rather than another `case`.

## Notes for reviewers

This is the first break the post-merge Docker workflow caught rather than prevented (#1077, #1083). The reporting half worked — #1107 opened six minutes after the first red and commented on the two runs after it.

jelen esetben a két állítás közül a makró a döntő, mert az magáról az elemről

author: extole-ada
body:
## What this changes

One new section on **What Happens When a Campaign Is Paused**, saying that pausing a campaign does not take it out of zone targeting, and that stopping it does.

The page today tells a reader that pausing "prevents new top-of-funnel traffic". That is true of promotion links and share flows, and it is not true of every zone. A paused campaign is still offered every zone request it publishes, and if no live campaign qualifies for that visitor it serves the zone, records the event against itself, and starts a journey for a visitor who had none.

## How to test this

Read the new section **A Paused Campaign Is Still a Targeting Candidate** on the branch preview. `npx mint@latest validate` passes (0 errors, 0 warnings).

Optional live check, on any account with a paused campaign that publishes the embedded-stats zone:

```
curl -sSI -H 'X-Extole-Debug: true' 'https://<program-domain>/zone/stats_embedded'
```

and read the `x-extole-log` lines `ZoneRenderService: rendered campaign: <id>` and `JourneyUpdateHandler_JOURNEY: creating/updating <journey> journey, with campaign=<id>`.

## Evidence

Measured 2026-09-11.

- On one production program domain, five consecutive signed-out requests for the embedded-stats zone were all served by campaigns that have been paused since 31 July, each one creating a `marketing` journey on the paused campaign for a visitor with zero journeys. The same visitor's microsite and share experience came from the live campaign.
- Those requests carried no campaign pin. Repeating them with `target=campaign_id:<the campaign that renders the page>` limited candidates to that campaign on all three attempts (`targeting candidates will be limited to this campaign=...`), rendered nothing, and opened no journey anywhere — which is why the second paragraph above names the pin. The same program's v10 microsite sends that pin on both embedded panels, so the exposure is on pages that do not: older microsites, and integrations calling a zone directly.
- On a test account, four of four signed-out requests for the same zone were served by a second live campaign and opened an `applicant` journey on it.

In pluribus, `ProductionSandboxRunningCampaignCache` keeps every campaign whose state is not `STOPPED`, so live, paused and ended campaigns are all targeting candidates; `CampaignFrontendControllersProvider` then filters each controller by `getEnabledOnStates().contains(campaignState)`, which is why the states a zone serves on are a property of the content block. The embedded-stats component in `extole/creative` declares `enabled_on_states: ["LIVE", "PAUSED"]` in both v8 and v10.

## What to look for — product

Whether "stop it" is the guidance we want to give, or whether the ask is a platform change so a brand-new visitor cannot enter a paused campaign at all. PROD-8799 is the same mechanism costing money on a friend journey, and TRIAG-2079 called new-visitor entry into a paused campaign a blocker back in 2017.

## What to look for — engineering

That the section is accurate and does not overreach: it says nothing about ended campaigns, which I did not measure.

## Ticket

None. Raised in #solutions-team while answering a question about `stats_embedded` zone attribution.

author: myshytf
body:
## What this changes

A hybrid engine that keeps its recurrent state on a checkpoint grid can only resume a follow-up prompt at the last hash boundary below the reused prefix, so every agentic turn recomputes the remainder of that unit plus the tokens the previous turn generated. Under `VLLM_K3_REQUEST_ENDPOINT_CACHE` a finished request publishes its **end position** as a prefix-cache entry — the attention page holding its last computed token, the pages of a speculative draft's sliding window, and one durable pool block per recurrent cache group carrying the state after that token. A later prompt whose tokens extend the producing sequence resumes there through the ordinary partial-hit copy-on-write path and computes only its new tokens.

Entry keys are the hash of the last whole unit below the end position; the lookup additionally verifies the remaining tail tokens and the request's extra keys, so a non-aligned end position is admitted only for a sequence that matches it exactly. Entries live in the block pool under an endpoint key in a separate group-id namespace, so eviction, reset and block reuse drop them together with the block they name, and `VLLM_K3_REQUEST_ENDPOINT_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES` (default 4) bounds the pool capacity they hold back.

Two properties are worth calling out:

- **One destination block per recurrent group.** One raw KV tensor is shared by one layer of every cache group, so a block id names the same physical page in each group. A single shared destination makes the groups' layers overwrite one another; the test suite pins this with groups whose layers share raw tensors.
- **A shadow for asynchronous scheduling.** The step after a request finishes is already in flight and overwrites its state slots, so the fused align pre-copy launch first snapshots every request's committed state into compact per-request shadow pages (conv window unshifted, temporal state per accepted speculative column). The materialization kernel then writes the durable blocks from those pages, or from the request's own blocks when no step is in flight, with the V1 copy-spec semantics.

`materialize_endpoints_torch` performs the same copies through per-state torch operations (`VLLM_K3_REQUEST_ENDPOINT_CACHE_TORCH_COPY`, or the file it names) and `verify_endpoints` compares a destination against that reference. With `VLLM_K3_REQUEST_ENDPOINT_CACHE_DEBUG` the first tensor-parallel rank verifies every materialization and logs the addresses the kernel resolved against the host expectation.

## Blast radius

Off by default. The scheduler disables it unless the model has recurrent layers in align mode with at most two concurrent batches, and the file named by `VLLM_K3_REQUEST_ENDPOINT_CACHE_DISABLE_FILE` switches registration and lookup off without a restart. An entry restores the end position of every cache group, a speculative draft's window included, so a deployment that hides restored KV from its draft group must keep the flag off. Model state v1 logs once and ignores the copies.

## Validation

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `tests/v1/core/prefix_cache/` (15 new endpoint cases) | 49 passed |
| `tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py`, `test_prefix_caching.py` | 20 failed, identical to the branch point (HF-config dependent) |
| Snapshot + materialization kernels through the Triton interpreter, 14 recurrent groups sharing one raw tensor | byte-identical for the kernel and the torch path; the resolved-address trace matches the host expectation; a shared destination corrupts 104 of 112 states |
| `tests/kernels/mamba/test_request_endpoint_shadow.py` | copy-spec equivalence, torch path, address trace, shared-raw-tensor groups, and a page geometry with conv and temporal views sharing 1,007,616-byte pages |

On a Kimi-K3 TP9/DCP9 deployment (93 layers, 69 recurrent, 4,608-token recurrent grid, 1,536-token hash unit, draft depth 3, two concurrent batches):

| Warm turn | Recomputed tokens | Time to first token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resumed at the end position | 18 | 0.37–0.62 s |
| Resumed at the last hash boundary | 118–606 | 0.35–0.58 s |
| Cold | full prompt | 1.9–4.9 s |

A document-recall oracle over 10 arms (stop-string and max_tokens producers, kernel and torch paths, aligned-path controls) reproduces the cold replay's greedy tokens with a largest per-token logprob difference of 1.1e-2, and every materialization on the serving engine verified byte-identical to its source. The end-position state is the one decode produced, so a cold prefill of the same tokens differs at that ~1e-2 level; resuming from a decode-reached boundary on the existing aligned path shows the same difference.

Costs on that deployment: the shadow reserves 842.6 MiB per GPU while the flag is on, and each entry pins one pool block per recurrent group (14 of 860 blocks).

author: thatstheend
body:
## TL;DR

every release ever published reported the SDK default `1.0.0`, same as a local debug build.

This PR fixes both halves:

- **Tags are validated.** `vX.Y.Z` only — lower-case `v`, three numbers. `scripts/Assert-ReleaseTag.ps1`
  runs first in the release workflow and refuses anything else with the specific mistake, why it
  matters, the intended tag and the retag commands. Five of the nine existing tags are upper-case
  (which the `v*` trigger ignores outright) and `v10.4` has two components.
- **Every install can say what it is.** The tag is stamped into the exe's version resource,
  `plugin.json` and a `VERSION.txt` at the archive root, and reported by `--version`, `lvai_status`
  and `pylv_status`. Plus a per-file manifest asset, so any install can be verified with no second
  install to compare against.

1667 tests pass (42 new). The README installer warning is removed — its premise doesn't hold.

---

A report that the plugin install "behaves differently" from the release-page download - specifically that its Python tooling was incomplete - was true as an observation and wrong as a diagnosis. Measured over one tag: the two routes are the same bytes by construction (the marketplace declares an `archive` source pointing at releases/latest/download/labview-mcp.zip), 732 files compared, every SHA-256 equal, the pylabview bundle byte-for-byte identical. The difference was version skew - a marketplace catalogue 13 days stale was serving a copy three releases behind.

Settling that took hashing 800 files, because nothing in an install carried a version: the csproj set no Version, so every release ever published reported the SDK default 1.0.0 and was indistinguishable from a local debug build. The commit SHA had been embedded the whole time (the SDK appends SourceRevisionId), so only the semantic half and the surfacing were missing.

Tag validation, the part that had to come first:

- scripts/Assert-ReleaseTag.ps1 accepts only vX.Y.Z - lower-case v, three decimal components - and is the FIRST step of the release workflow, so a bad tag costs seconds and publishes nothing. Each refusal names the actual mistake (upper-case V, missing v, two components, four, a -rc/+meta suffix, a non-numeric part, a leading zero), why it matters, the probable intended tag, and the delete-and-retag commands. Five of the nine existing tags are upper-case - which git treats as a different ref, so the v* trigger ignores them outright - and v10.4 has two components, which additionally sorts above every three-part tag in `git tag --sort=-v:refname`.
- Leading zeros are refused too: MSBuild reads 02 as 2, so v1.02.3 and v1.2.3 would stamp an identical version while remaining different git refs.
- ReleaseTagTests drives the real script rather than re-stating its regex, and asserts the message names the mistake and that each suggestion is itself accepted.

Version stamping and surfacing:

- <Version>0.0.0</Version> marks a build that did not come from the workflow; the workflow passes -p:Version=<tag> to the Release build and the publish, and asserts the stamp landed rather than assuming it.
- ServerVersion reads InformationalVersion; reported by a new --version flag, by lvai_status and by pylv_status - that last one because it is the only one that answers with no LabVIEW running, including on its notProvisioned path.
- plugin.json carries a 0.0.0 placeholder substituted at staging, so `claude plugin list` can identify the plugin.
- VERSION.txt at the archive root, because a file NAME dies at extraction: it is what lets a hand-extracted folder say what it is.

Release assets: the fixed-name labview-mcp.zip stays (the marketplace resolves it), plus a version-named copy, its SHA-256, and a per-file manifest that lets any install be verified with no second install to compare against.

Also: scripts/Compare-Installs.ps1, which is the comparison above, with a -ManifestPath mode and a negative control; docs/release-versioning.md with the measurements; and the README installer warning removed, since the premise behind it does not hold.

One defect found by dry-running the stamping step locally rather than trusting it: the readback used `Get-Content -Raw`, which decodes a BOM-less file with the system ANSI codepage on Windows PowerShell, turning the non-ASCII author name to mojibake. Every read and write in that step now states its encoding, and the result is asserted byte-identical to what was meant.

author: agentiknet
body:
## Why

`pnpm lint` has been broken in this repo. It runs `next lint`, a subcommand
Next.js **16 removed**, and the repo carries no eslint config at all. So the
script just errors — and no workflow ever called it. **Nothing has been linted
here for months.**

## What

Migrate to the setup Next 16 expects — `eslint` + `eslint-config-next` via
`eslint.config.mjs` (flat config).

- **`eslint.config.mjs`** — `eslint-config-next` 16 ships flat configs
  natively, so no `@eslint/eslintrc` `FlatCompat` shim. `core-web-vitals` +
  `typescript` are the flat equivalent of the legacy
  `extends: ["next/core-web-vitals", "next/typescript"]`.
  **Byte-identical with the site sibling** — the two repos share components
  and scripts.
- **`reportUnusedDisableDirectives: "error"`** — a suppression can no longer
  outlive the rule it suppresses. That is precisely how this rotted, and it
  applies in editors too, which a CLI flag would not. It immediately earned
  its keep (see below).
- **`lint` script** → `eslint . --max-warnings=0`.
- **CI** now runs `pnpm lint` (source-only, needs no content sync), so it
  cannot go silently non-functional again. Job renamed to
  `Lint + type-check + build`; `main` has no branch protection, so no required
  check name is disturbed.

## Violations surfaced — 14 errors, 1 warning

**Fixed:**

- **Two dead `no-control-regex` suppressions** (`SessionChatView.tsx:67`,
  `ToolBlocks.tsx:59`) — that rule is not part of `eslint-config-next`, so
  those comments never suppressed anything. Removed. If we want the guard on
  these ANSI-stripping regexes it is a one-line `rules` addition; left out to
  keep the config vanilla-Next. Say the word and I will add it.
- `react/no-unescaped-entities` — escaped an apostrophe in
  `SessionChatView.tsx`.
- `@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars` — dropped the unused `ev` param on the
  PTY socket `close` handler.

**Re-scoped, not fixed** — `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` and
`react-hooks/refs` turned off in the config, with the rationale written into
the file:

These are React-Compiler-era advisories, new in `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`
v7 (pulled in by `eslint-config-next` 16). They are performance advice, not
correctness bugs. They flag ~11 sites across `panel/page.tsx`,
`SessionChatView.tsx`, `use-daemon.ts` and `use-session-events.ts` — the
reset-state-on-session-change effects and the refs mirrored during render that
the daemon panel is built on. Converting those is a behavioural refactor of a
live interactive UI and belongs in its own PR where it can actually be
exercised against a running daemon — not as a rider on a lint migration.

Happy to split that follow-up out if you want it tracked as an issue.

## Verification

- `pnpm lint` → exit 0, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 unused directives
- `tsc --noEmit` → exit 0

## Not in scope

The site repos have no committed lockfile (CI installs with
`--no-frozen-lockfile`); they resolve from the agentik-studio root lockfile,
where the two new devDeps land as a separate commit.

## Coordination

Sibling PR: agentproto/site — same branch name, identical
`eslint.config.mjs`. Merge together.

Independent of the in-flight copy-only PR #10 (`copy/facts-refresh-2026-09`);
this branched from `origin/main`.

## ⚠️ CI is red for an unrelated, pre-existing reason

The new **Lint** step passes. So does **Type-check**. The **Build** step fails —
and it already failed before this branch existed:

- this PR: `./content/docs/guides/sandbox-rendezvous.mdx` `29:2: Unexpected
  character '!'`
- copy-only PR #10, same failure, same file, same line

`prebuild` clones `agentproto/ts@main` into `content/docs/` at build time, so
the site build tracks upstream CLI docs. `sandbox-rendezvous.mdx` has drifted
into MDX that `fumadocs-mdx` rejects (a `<!-- -->` HTML comment, which MDX does
not accept). Last green run on `main` here was 2026-07-12.

That means **the site build — and therefore the deploy — is currently broken
independently of lint.** It needs a fix in `agentproto/ts`, not here.
Tracking separately.

author: patelkrish099
body:
### Motivation

- Provide a production-oriented, security-first rework of the bot panel with strict per-user and per-bot isolation enforced server-side. 
- Ensure dependencies/installations are performed inside each bot’s own runtime (never globally) and surface installation/logs clearly to users. 
- Replace the placeholder UI with a polished Python-only WebApp on port `5069` that exposes secure file management, terminal, runtime controls and live logs for each isolated workspace.

### Description

- Add a new Flask application (`app.py`) implementing signed server-side authentication (`/auth/*`), per-user catalogs, per-bot UUID ownership checks, rate limiting, audit logs, and robust error handling. 
- Implement Docker-backed isolation where each bot gets three dedicated Docker volumes (files, data, runtime) and a constrained container with `--network none`, capability drops, `no-new-privileges`, pids/memory/cpu limits, and `docker cp` based content transfers. 
- Provide secure file operations and tooling: safe POSIX path normalization (`safe_path`), file read/write/upload/download, folder create/delete/rename, search, ZIP creation/extraction with ZIP-Slip protections, text/binary size limits, and audit events. 
- Add runtime controls and safe process management: `start/stop/restart` that install `requirements.txt` inside the container’s venv, run the bot in a detached process with PID tracking (`/runtime/bot.pid`), and store install/start logs under `/runtime` per-bot. 
- Add a restricted terminal API with an explicit allowlist and parsing/validation to prevent shell escapes, and implement `exec_in`/`cp_out` helpers that always operate inside the bot container. 
- Ship a modern premium UI: `templates/panel.html`, `static/panel.css`, and `static/panel.js` implementing bot list, file explorer/editor, upload/download/rename/search, terminal, live logs, runtime buttons, confirmations, toasts and responsive theming. 
- Include `README.md` and `requirements.txt` documenting deployment, server-side Telegram panel link flow (`panel_link_for_telegram`) and the deliberate fail-closed policy if Docker is unavailable.

### Testing

- Ran `python -m py_compile app.py` to ensure the Python code parses and compiles (success). 
- Ran `node --check static/panel.js` to validate the shipped client-side JS (success). 
- Ran `git diff --check` and static checks to validate whitespace/formatting (success). 
- Attempted `pip install -r requirements.txt` inside a venv but package install could not complete because the CI environment’s proxy blocked PyPI access (not a code failure). 
- `docker` was unavailable in this environment so full integration tests for container creation, `requirements.txt` installation inside containers, runtime execution, and `docker cp` transfers could not be exercised here (manual/CI runtime validation required).

body:
## What changed

Version goes to 1.1.0 in the six manifests the release workflow validates
against the tag, and `.github/CHANGELOG.md` gains a `## 1.1.0 - 2026-09-11`
section covering the memory classes merged in #1. No skill text changes.

## Why

The bump is minor, not patch, because memory entries gained a class and a
promotion ladder, which is new behavior an upgrader will see. It is not major
because an existing store keeps working: the consolidation pass adds the
missing class the next time it runs, and no entry is deleted for lacking one.
The changelog says so, since that is the only question an upgrader has.

Six files rather than three: `kimi.plugin.json`, `qwen-extension.json`, and
`package.json` also carry a version and are checked by the workflow's version
gate. Bumping only the three obvious plugin manifests would have failed the
tag. The two marketplace manifests have no version field and stay untouched.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 skills/black-iris/scripts/universal/check.py   # clean

VER=1.1.0
for f in .claude-plugin/plugin.json .codex-plugin/plugin.json kimi.plugin.json \
         qwen-extension.json gemini-extension.json package.json; do
  python3 -c "import json,sys; print(sys.argv[1], json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))['version'])" "$f"
done
grep -nE "^## \[?$VER\]?( |$)" .github/CHANGELOG.md
```

The release workflow's notes step was also extracted from `release.yml` and
run verbatim against this changelog. It emits the 1.1.0 section and the
install footer, and stops at the 1.0.0 heading.

## Out of scope

The `allowed-tools` note in #1 overstated the problem. The 1.0.0 changelog
records the four-tool grant as deliberate, with Bash, Write, and Edit going
through the harness permission prompt. That claim is still unverified against
a real harness and is worth confirming separately, now that the episodic
write is frequent.

author: wyx-sg
body:
## What

`coffer__search` resolves an implicit scope across project + global (`span="both"`). `coffer__grep` and `coffer__read` stayed single-scope, so the three retrieval tools disagreed about what "no scope argument" means.

Two consequences, both reachable from a normal agent session inside a git project:

- **`read` could not read back what `search` returned.** A hit from the global store came back with an id, but `coffer__read(id)` resolved to the project scope and raised `MemoryNotFound`. The search tool's own description — "pass an id to coffer__read for the full text" — was false for those hits.
- **`grep` silently missed global.** Grepping an exact identifier from inside a project searched only that project's store.

## Change

Both now span the same way `search` does, at the surface layer:

- `read` resolves in the project scope and falls back to `global` on `MemoryNotFound` / `DocumentNotFound`, reporting the scope it actually read from.
- `grep` queries the project store, then global with the remaining `max_matches` budget, marking `truncated` when the project alone filled the budget.

An explicit `scope` stays literal in both: never folded, never fallen back from. `global` never queries itself twice.

`KnowledgeService` keeps its one-store-at-a-time semantics — whether to span is the tool layer's decision, matching where `search` already makes it.

## Tests

Four integration tests in `test_entry_scope_tools.py`, next to the existing `test_search_spans_project_and_global_by_default`: one span test and one explicit-scope test for each of `read` and `grep`.

body:
Implements the marketplace deal flow agreed after Market Method v2.

Core flow:
- structured offers in Messages: full asking price, -10%, -20%, custom and counteroffers
- explicit `Offer accepted` state that is NOT market evidence
- seller follow-up after 3 days: Sale completed / Not yet / Cancelled
- final item price stored separately from optional shipping
- buyer confirmation or dispute
- only bilateral confirmed sales enter Market Method v2 as verified completed-sale evidence
- historical ECB conversion for non-EUR confirmed sales when available
- confirmed TrackDash sales also feed chronological monthly trend evidence
- repeated same buyer/seller pair activity is capped into 30-day independent evidence clusters
- one physical collection share can have only one live accepted deal across conversations
- a reserved share cannot be removed/edited while a live accepted deal is pending
- message badge includes due sale follow-ups and pending buyer confirmations

Automatic ownership transfer on bilateral confirmation:
- exactly one physical copy leaves the seller's active collection
- if the seller row represents multiple identical copies, quantity is decremented by one
- buyer automatically receives a new collection row with quantity 1, confirmed condition, sale date/item price/currency and acquisition source `TrackDash`
- shipping stays separate and never becomes the buyer's market item price
- seller ownership data and photo URLs are preserved in immutable `collection_item_transfers` history
- the old public listing is removed; the conversation safely keeps its transaction history with a null share reference

Database:
- `0071_marketplace_offer_sale_flow.sql`
- `0072_marketplace_deal_reservation_guards.sql`
- `0073_marketplace_collection_transfer.sql`
- participant-read RLS with state mutations through guarded SECURITY DEFINER functions
- `trackdash_confirmed_sales` first-party price source

Validation:
- production Supabase migrations 0071-0073 applied successfully
- full offer -> accepted -> seller report -> buyer confirm -> ownership transfer smoke path passed inside a rollback transaction
- buyer collection row, seller removal/decrement, transfer history and listing removal were explicitly asserted
- rollback verified: no test offer/sale/transfer persisted
- latest available Vercel preview gates pass, including R3 13/13, Market Method v1 12/12, Market Method v2 10/10 and public surfaces 8/8

## 결정된 정책 (이슈의 "결정 필요" 항목)

- 한 글에 동시에 유효한(대기중/수락됨) 신청은 1인 1건만 — 중복 신청 차단
- 글쓴이는 한 글에서 여러 명을 수락할 수 있음(마감 전까지 계속 열려있음)
- 반려된 신청자는 같은 글에 다시 신청 가능(이력은 남김) — 글쓴이가 "예전에 신청했던 사람"인지 알 수 있도록 신청자 목록에 "재신청" 뱃지 표시(닉네임을 바꿔도 계정 고정 식별자 기준이라 가려낼 수 있음)

## 변경 사항

**서버 (`server/services/communityService.js`, `server/routes/community.js`)**
- `applyToPost`/`getMyApplications`/`getApplicantsForPost`/`decideApplication`/`closePost`/`editPost`/`deletePostByAuthor` 추가
- 신청 가능 여부(승인됨+본인 글 아님+마감 안 됨)는 기존 `getPostById`를 그대로 재사용해 판정 — 목록/상세 노출 규칙과 항상 같은 기준을 쓰게 함
- `closePost`는 마감 시점 대기 중이던 신청을 자동 반려(이슈 명세)
- 새 라우트: `POST /:id/apply`, `GET /applications/mine`, `GET /:id/applications`, `POST /applications/:id/accept|reject`, `POST /:id/close`, `PATCH /:id`, `DELETE /:id`

**클라이언트 (`client/src/pages/Community.jsx`, `chatApi.js`, `App.css`)**
- "내 신청" 탭 추가
- 상세 뷰가 남의 글(신청 폼/상태별 안내+재신청)과 내 글(신청자 목록+수락/반려+재신청 뱃지+마감/수정/삭제 버튼)로 분기
- 글쓰기 폼을 수정 모드로도 재사용

## 검증

두 계정(글쓴이/신청자 역할)을 오가며 로컬에서 전체 플로우 직접 검증:
- 신청 → 대기중 표시 → 같은 글에 중복 신청 시도 → `409 DUPLICATE_APPLICATION`
- 수락 → 신청자/글쓴이 양쪽에 연락 이메일 공개 확인
- 반려 → 재신청 허용 확인 → 신청자 목록에 "재신청" 뱃지 확인(서버 응답 직접 확인 + UI 스크린샷)
- 모집 마감 → 대기 중이던 신청 자동 반려 확인, 마감 후 신청 시도 → `400 POST_CLOSED`
- 본인 글에 신청 시도 → `400 CANNOT_APPLY_OWN_POST`
- 승인된 글 수정 → 상태가 pending으로 바뀌어 공개 목록에서 사라지는 것 확인, 기존 신청 데이터는 그대로 유지되는 것 확인
- 삭제 → 상태 무관 항상 가능, 삭제 후 404 확인
- 다크/라이트 모드 스크린샷 확인
- `npm run lint --workspace=client` 통과

author: salmanmuddhoo
body:
## What this changes

Four pieces of officer feedback:

**1. Bug: re-uploading after a rejection silently deleted the new file again.** After deleting a rejected document and uploading its replacement, the page kept showing no View button for the new file, the KYC chevron kept counting it as outstanding, and Next stayed disabled — the officer had to leave and come back to the page. Root cause: the delete button is a plain form POST with no redirect afterwards, so the browser's "current entry" for the page was that POST. `window.location.reload()` (called once the replacement finished uploading) replays whatever entry it is called on verbatim — method and body included — so it silently *resubmitted the delete*, taking the just-uploaded file straight back out. Fixed on all three application pages ([id].astro, account.astro, customer.astro) by navigating to the current URL instead of reloading, which always issues a fresh GET regardless of what the previous request was.

**2. The printable form's signature page didn't say what was being opened.** It named the applicant's membership type ("Individual"/"Corporate") instead of the account. Now reads e.g. *"Application for Membership — Shares and Multiplier Savings Account"* or *"Application form — Hajj Savings Account"*, built from the configured account types (membership-default types for a membership application, the selected type(s) for an account application) rather than hardcoded text.

**3. Test and Production were writing into the same SharePoint tree.** Nothing told a preview upload apart from a real member's identity documents. `ROOT_FOLDER` is now split by the same `PUBLIC_APP_ENV` signal the TEST badge already reads (`isProductionEnvironment` — unset treated as production, same as everywhere else that signal gates something). Each side creates its own root automatically on the next document filed there; nothing to provision by hand.

**4. SharePoint folders reorganised to be named by applicant.** An application's folder is now named after its applicant — surname, first name, with the reference trailing (`Applications/Ramtoola Yusuf – AB-000042`) — instead of a bare reference, so an officer can recognise whose documents are inside without opening it. Still exactly one folder per person, not per application: the existing `folder_application_id` consolidation (an additional account or a converting non-member reuses their founding application's own folder) is unchanged, only what that shared folder is *named* is. Applies going forward only — nothing already filed in SharePoint is moved or renamed, and `deleteDraftApplication` now reads the same applicant name under the same lock so a deleted draft's discard targets the folder its own files were actually filed under.

## Related

Officer feedback on the review/document workflow, the printable form, and SharePoint organisation.

## Checks

- [x] Type-check and production build pass locally (`pnpm build`)
- [x] Formatting applied (`pnpm format:fix`)
- [x] No credentials, tokens or connection strings added to the repository
- [x] Permissions enforced for any new route or API endpoint
- [x] Audit trail written for any change to member, document, approval or payment data
- [ ] Documentation updated where behaviour changed

## Security considerations

No new routes, endpoints, permissions or schema. The reload fix is purely client-side navigation. The SharePoint folder-naming and environment-root changes touch only where files are written going forward — nothing already filed is read differently or moved. `deleteDraftApplication`'s discard path now reads the applicant's own name fresh, under the same row lock already used for the delete, rather than trusting a caller-supplied value. Full suite (**722 tests**, 4 new), build, route and OpenAPI checks pass; no migration.

author: fchecklist
body:
## F-034/F-036: capability-tree duplicate fetch

**Bug (already root-caused before this PR, see task context):** a single page mount fetched the identical construction capability tree from the ct backend TWICE, concurrently:
1. Once inside `/api/shell`'s own fan-out (F-21/R-236 — deliberately batches this exact read into one `Promise.allSettled` to avoid redundant per-page fetches).
2. Once again, unconditionally, from `veri-chat-context.tsx`'s `fetchCapabilityTree()`, which called `fetch("/api/capability-tree")` on every mount without ever consulting `shell-store.ts`'s already-fetched `capabilityTree` field.

A real Playwright trace showed 5 concurrent GETs within 626ms of a `/scope/new` mount, contributing to 7-9+ concurrent `withTenantContext` connections against ct's 5-connection pool and a real 504 (the save POST then timing out at 9.75s) — blocking real test closure for Sumeet requirements R-11 and R-B2.

## Fix

`fetchCapabilityTree()` now routes through a new internal `fetchConstructionTree()`:

1. **Warm shell cache** — if `/api/shell` already has a fresh tree this session, use it directly. Zero network.
2. **In-flight join** — if a shell bootstrap is already running (started by `M24Shell`'s own `useShell()`), await that SAME request and read the tree from it instead of firing a second one.
3. **Fallback** — neither of the above: fetch `/api/capability-tree` directly, exactly as before this fix.

Two new passive-read exports back this in `shell-store.ts`: `getFreshShellCapabilityTree()` and `getInFlightShellLoad()`. Neither **starts** a shell load — this is deliberate. `M24Shell.tsx`'s F-19 withholds the shell bootstrap on a create route (`/new`, `/upload`, `/log-time`) until the form's own critical-path reads finish; calling `loadShell()` unconditionally from the composer would defeat that on exactly the routes it protects.

On a **non-create route**, the join is deterministic, not a timing race: React commits a descendant's mount effects before its ancestor's, and `M24Shell` is a descendant of `VeriChatProvider` in `app/(app)/layout.tsx` — so `M24Shell`'s `loadShell()` call has already set the in-flight promise by the time `VeriChatProvider`'s own effect (which calls `fetchCapabilityTree()`) runs.

On a **cold load of a create route** specifically, neither a warm cache nor an in-flight request exists yet at mount, so this falls back to the original direct fetch, unchanged from today's behavior. This is a known, scoped limitation — see the code comment in `fetchConstructionTree()` for why extending the fix there would mean touching F-19's own deferral logic, which felt like a separate, riskier decision than this PR should make.

## Blast radius

`shell-store.ts`'s diff is **purely additive** — confirmed via `git diff` showing zero removed/modified lines — so no other of its ~10 existing callers (`M24Shell.tsx`, `RosterCreateClient.tsx`, `ProjectCreateClient.tsx`, `MaterialReceiptCreateClient.tsx`, `LabourClient.tsx`, `DashboardSpeculation.tsx`, `AttendanceCreateClient.tsx`, ...) changes behavior. `VeriComposer.tsx`'s consumption of `tree`/`treeLoading` is untouched — the shared factory (`create-veri-chat-context.tsx`) still owns `treeLoading`'s lifecycle exactly as before; only where the underlying data comes from changed.

## Testing

- Extended `veri-chat-context.test.ts` with 3 new cases: baseline (no shell data → direct fetch, unchanged), warm-cache hit (zero calls to `/api/capability-tree`), and in-flight join (one real network call total, not two).
- **Verify-then-revert** (R74-RULING-03-style discipline): temporarily reverted `fetchCapabilityTree()`'s call site back to the old `fetchJsonNodes("/api/capability-tree")` (via `git stash` on just that file) — both new regression tests failed as expected (wrong tree source; `shellCalls` was 2, not 1). Reapplied the fix — both pass again. `git diff` confirmed empty before the final commit.
- `bun test --isolate`: **4142 pass / 0 fail across 310 files** (full suite).
- `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint` both clean on the whole project / changed files.

Not merging this myself per the task's instructions.

body:
## What this changes

- **Changes tab**: the status letter moves from the row head to the row end, right-aligned (`ml-auto`) into one fixed-width column — the VS Code Source Control layout. The file name is now the first thing on a row, flush with sibling directory names in the tree view.
- **Files tab**: gets the same decorations. File rows reuse `StatusBadge`; directory rows get a dot plus a tinted name when anything under them changed (conflict wins, then modified, deleted, added, untracked).

| Changes (list / tree) | Files |
|---|---|
| `web.md  docs/design ………… M` | `docs ……………………… ●` / `ChangeList.tsx … M` |

## Why

The letter at the row head pushed every file name one column to the right and, in the tree view, out of line with directory names. The Files tab had no way to see where the changes were without switching tabs.

Mechanism: one `codeByPath` table in `state/store.ts` feeds both kinds of row — every status entry claims its own path and all ancestors, merged by a fixed precedence. Claiming the entry's own path is what makes submodules work without a special case (git records their change on the gitlink path). The three badges share one `STATUS_SLOT` constant so the column width is structural. `fileByPath` is gone (no consumers left).

Design notes are in `docs/design/web.md` (变更列表 / 文件浏览器).
