author: zmainen
body:
Item 5 of the plan in #56. The edge prompt was 1.7 KB: it named nine CiTO/claimrel types with one gloss each, no direction rule and no example, and gave the model the claims truncated at 220 characters with no evidence and no paper text. Five relations the corpus uses — `validates`, `confirms`, `extends`, `refutes`, `qualifies` — could not be emitted at all, and `part-of` post-dated it. On the recorded Gädeke run it returned 75 edges dominated by `requires` and `scopes`, with the deductive spine thin.

This rebuilds edge inference on the contract.

## The prompt on the contract

- `extract/prompts/edge-inference.md` is rewritten as a one-page task in the style of the reader tasks — no persona, no numbered failure modes. It asks for one edge per line as `{"source": n, "target": m, "relation": "…", "why": "…"}`, in the corpus's own vocabulary (not CiTO); the direction rules in the vocabulary are binding; `derived-from` and `confirms` are never emitted; `rules-out` may only target an `entertains`/`rejects` claim; `part-of` is composition, not support; and it is better to miss an edge than to invent one.
- The layer now reads `contract/vocabulary.md` — added to `prompts.ROLES` and to the layer's `reads:` in `pipeline/layers.yaml` — so the relations, their directions and the confusable pairs come from `scripts/relations.py`, and the prompt and the checker read one rule. The prompt-composition test holds the two equal.

## What the model is given

`edges._claim_digest` now renders, per claim: number, role, panel, stance, the full claim sentence, its cited spans where the draft records any, and every evidence quote from `evidence_by_agent` in full (not truncated to 220 characters). The numbered-reference convention and `_resolve` are kept.

## Validation with direction checks

`CITO_TO_CORPUS` is gone; the vocabulary is loaded from `relations.py` the way `contract.py` does. Each edge is rejected, with a logged reason, when: the relation or a reference is unknown or self-referential; `derived-from`/`confirms` is emitted; `tests` does not run empirical/control → prediction; `entails` is not from a hypothesis; `rules-out`/`contradicts`/`opposes` targets a claim the paper asserts (the `CONTRARY` set `check_relations.py` enforces, imported so the two agree); `scopes` is not from a scope claim; `part-of` would form a cycle or a second whole; or `dissociates-with` is written twice for one pair. `derived-from` and `confirms` are synthesised as the reciprocals of `entails` and `predicts`. Each edge's `why` is recorded in the output and written into the claim body under a Relations note — the frontmatter shape is unchanged.

## Chunking

An optional `--per-arc` flag dumps or asks one request per hypothesis arc (the hypothesis, its predictions and the claims that mention them) and merges the answers through the same validation. Default off.

## The Gädeke run

Answered by a subagent (Claude Opus 4.8) against the recorded external-review v2 draft and recorded with `pipeline.py run … --answer` (the tree stays at v2; `claim-tree` was not run):

| | v3 (recorded) | this run |
|---|--:|--:|
| edges | 75 | 78 |
| relation types | 8 | 12 |

By relation: `supports` 16, `requires` 16, `scopes` 9, `tests` 8, `entails` 5, `part-of` 5, `derived-from` 5, `interprets` 4, `enables-method` 4, `validates` 4, `dissociates-with` 1, `qualifies` 1. Relations unreachable from the old prompt (`validates`, `qualifies`, `part-of`) now appear; the spine is explicit rather than thin.

- **Rejected by the validator: 0** — the answer was written to the contract, so nothing broke a direction rule.
- **Spans in `why`: 0** — the recorded external-review draft predates span-cited evidence and carries none, so the digest showed no span id to cite. The digest surfaces spans when the draft has them (covered by test); this run's upstream simply does not.
- **Deductive spine:** every one of the four hypotheses now carries an `entails` to at least one prediction, and every one of the five predictions is the target of a `tests`.

## Tests and gates

New tests cover each rejection rule (one case each), reciprocal synthesis, the `why` carried through to the body and kept out of the frontmatter, `part-of` cycle and second-whole rejection, and the prompt-composition test for the new `reads`. Gates pass: `make check` (including `check_relations.py`), both test files standalone from `extract/`, `make data`, `make fresh`.

## Left open

- No `why` in this run cites a span, because the recorded external-review draft predates spans (plan item 3). Re-running edge inference on a draft that carries spans is what will exercise that path end to end.
- Freshly drafted claims carry no stance, so `_stance` defaults to `asserts` and `rules-out` has no valid target in the induction chain — as designed, the alternatives it eliminates are raised by the `stance` layer and carried over. If a reviewer is later given a way to mark an alternative `entertains`, edge inference could emit `rules-out` directly.

Closes #83

author: askalf
body:
## Resume on the same model first; the other provider is the second hop

Follow-up to #1286. 6.1.0 knew one continuation target — the other provider's `--pool-fallback` entry — so a user with one plan and no chain got nothing, and a user with both got a model swap for what is usually a transient reset.

**First choice: the model the client asked for**, as a fresh request through dario's own front door. The pool picks a seat (sticky binding keeps the prompt cache warm), and if the provider cannot take the request at all the existing pre-byte failover already hands it to the other one. This is what most dying streams get, and it works with one plan.

**Second choice: the other provider's chain entry**, taken when the first delivers nothing (refused, unreachable, dead before its first byte) or when the resume itself dies mid-way. In the second case the resume's own guard makes the hop, so the client stream carries two seam comments:

```
: dario continuation claude-opus-5 (same model) after 309 chars
: dario continuation gpt-5.6-terra (codex fleet) after 300 chars
```

`x-dario-continuation` now carries the depth; depth 2 is never continued — two hops, never three. A guard on a depth-1 request skips choice 1 (that model just failed twice). The log names who served each continuation (`continuation done by claude-opus-5: +1451 chars …`).

## Evidence

- `test/midstream.mjs` 93 (choices in order; depth-1 guard starts at choice 2; every choice refused → `resume-failed`; inner seam comment forwarded; `continuationDepth`).
- `test/midstream-continuation-wiring.mjs` 43 — rewritten around per-request plans so each scenario states what the primary, the same-model resume, and the other provider do: same-model resume on both wire shapes; same-model refused → other provider; same-model dies → second hop inside the resume, both seams on the client stream; codex `response.failed` → codex again; codex fails twice → Claude pool; nobody left for the second hop → left unfinished; `tool_use` cut, flag off, depth 2. Requests dario makes on its own (probes) no longer consume a plan entry — the earlier version was order-sensitive to them.
- Full suite 199/199.
- **Live on the box** through this build (second instance sharing the store, chaos taps on the real Anthropic stream and a relay on the real codex stream): same-model resumes **4/4** — Opus 5 → Opus 5, GPT-5.6-sol → GPT-5.6-sol, prose and code, anchor exact:
  ```
  …the other end acknowledges what<CUT> it has received. The catch is that both directions…
  …confirm that it has received the other side's<CUT> sequence number. This establishes…
  ```
  and the forced two-hop **2/2** — Opus dies, Opus resume dies, GPT-5.6-terra finishes it; GPT dies, GPT resume dies, Sonnet 5 finishes it — each one valid message with two seams.

## Trade-offs

- A same-model resume usually lands on the seat that just died (sticky binding). If that seat is the problem rather than the connection, the cost is one wasted hop before the other provider; the pool learns nothing from a mid-stream death because no headers come back with it.
- Two hops means up to two extra requests; the live two-hop cases stalled the client ~13–22 s total.
- Bumped to 6.2.0 in-PR.

author: lsm
body:
The configured shared catalog now exposes `task.start` for direct execution and verified terminal-task retries. RPC/internal callers and active persisted MCP sessions in the owning Space use one pipeline to persist a claim and its linked start job; the response is a durable acknowledgement, with no inline SDK startup.

Input is only `taskId` and `requestKey`. Replaying a request uses its frozen persisted input; a new retry derives the previous attempt/generation from current task ownership and preserves the existing lifecycle guards and reopen callback. Workflow tasks and review rejection remain on their existing interfaces. Use a stable key for the same request and a new key for a new execution.

Merge contract: one shared start/retry control and trivial configured registration, using existing stages. No schema, guardian, duplicate transport handler, or new infrastructure. The merged shared review-rejection route remains available before this public entry point.

Revised review-fix budgets: 300 production / 440 test changed lines. The capacity correction extracts the existing workflow scheduler policy and checks it inside the direct activation transaction; queued starts wait without starting SDK work when capacity is occupied. Regression coverage includes concurrent direct starts and all existing counted task states.

Validation: fresh-dev rebase, frozen install, and `bun run check` passed. Tests execute in CI only; no internal review passes. Coverage includes shared transport acknowledgement, caller scope, derived terminal retry identities, idempotence, reopen callback, and lazy capability registration. Existing connected completion tests remain in the CI suite.

Closes #4382. Part of #4164.

Workflow/direct interleaving correction: workflow spawning now reserves the canonical task status before awaiting its SDK spawn, sharing the same atomic capacity accounting with direct activation. Failed unstarted reservations release only when the exact workflow/lifecycle ownership still matches; tests cover an interleaved direct start and superseded cleanup. This extends the same public capacity-admission fix without infrastructure.

Attachment admission now joins the existing pinned-run transaction, so its parent task status and run binding consume capacity together. Additional CI cases cover a direct start winning before attachment commits and a multi-agent partial success retaining its start timestamp.

Persisted workflow reservations now stamp missing start metadata after successful recovery spawning, guarded by the exact pre-spawn lifecycle generation/run/status and preserving any existing timestamp. CI regression variants cover missing, existing, and superseded start generations. Final measured 300 production / 429 test changed lines.

author: zhuyue11
body:
Closes MOTIR-5191.

`ApprovalGateControl` has rendered `Waiting on {name}.` since MOTIR-4792 and has never been handed a name. Both production mounts passed a literal `routedToLabel={null}`, so every reader who may *see* a gate but not *decide* it read the generic fallback — *"Waiting on this work item's assignee."* — and never a person.

## What was wrong, and why nothing caught it

The seam was complete except for its last inch: the id is on the gate, the prop is on the component, the sentence is in both locales, and **three component tests assert that sentence renders with a name in it**. All three were green on the defect, because they pass the name in themselves. A test that hands a component its input cannot discover that no caller ever does — so the fix is only half the work, and the guard below is the other half.

## The fix

- **`lib/approvalGates/routing.ts` (new)** — ADR §2's routing rule and the display-name rule, stated once. `designResultHandler.routeTo` now delegates to the first; the item page and the Approvals queue both use them.
- **`approvalGatesService.getForWorkItem`** returns `routedToLabel` beside `canDecide`, resolved from the kind's own `routeTo` on the item it already has in hand.
- **The Approvals queue** carries `routedToName` per row, resolved **once per page** via a batched `findByIds` — the same discipline `summarizeGateSubjects` keeps one read up.
- **Both mounts** now pass a real label.

## ⚠️ A falsified premise: criterion 2 named the wrong column

**The card asked for the name to be resolved from `routedToId`. It is resolved from the LIVE routing answer instead, and the criterion is amended on the record.**

`routedToId` is written at gate **creation** and is the AUDIT record of who was *asked* — ADR §6a says so outright (*"§2's answer computed at creation; the assignee can change afterwards"*), and `docs/decisions/approval-gates.md` §3 is an explicit decision that this column carries **no surviving label**, unlike `decidedById`.

The sentence it would feed is **present tense**, and its reader's next act is to go and ask somebody. On a reassigned card the frozen column names a person who no longer sees the gate at all. `approvalGateRepository` had already ruled on exactly this question, in code that merged **after this card was written**:

> a different question — *whose job is it to look, now* — and answering it from the frozen column would strand every gate on a reassigned card in the previous assignee's tab. […] The audit column and this predicate are both right, about different questions.

So the card's **outcome** stands in full and its **mechanism** does not. The divergence is pinned by a test (`tracks a REASSIGNMENT`), which asserts the label follows the reassignment *while* `routedToId` stays where it was. Planning bug filed under MOTIR-1465.

## ⚠️ The enumeration drifted: one call site became two

The card says *"the only production caller"*, measured at `65116fb19`. On `origin/main` there are **two**:

```
$ git grep -n "routedToLabel={null}" origin/main
origin/main:app/(authed)/items/[key]/_components/DesignResultSection.tsx:172
origin/main:app/(authed)/workbench/_components/ApprovalsList.tsx:361
```

Dated rather than assumed — `git log --diff-filter=A` puts `ApprovalsList.tsx` at **2026-09-11T19:46:57Z** (MOTIR-4879, the Approvals tab), against the card's `createdAt` of **17:53**. It **postdates** the card, so this is genuine drift and not a count that was wrong when written: the Approvals tab copied the hardcoded `null` from the only example it had, roughly two hours after the bug reporting it was filed. The card's criteria already anticipated this (*"every surface that renders `ApprovalGateControl`"*), so both are fixed here.

## Criterion 5 — the test asserts the WIRING

`tests/approval-gate-routed-to-wiring.test.ts` enumerates every production file that **mounts** the frame (imports the module *and* renders the element) and asserts none hardcodes the prop to `null`. It quantifies over whatever mounts the frame today rather than over a list — a guard naming one file would have gone green while the defect doubled — and it asserts the site list is non-empty so a rename cannot make it pass vacuously.

**Verified red before the fix**, at both sites:

```
× DesignResultSection.tsx does NOT hardcode routedToLabel to null — the defect itself
× ApprovalsList.tsx does NOT hardcode routedToLabel to null — the defect itself
  AssertionError: … passes routedToLabel={null} — the frame will draw its generic fallback
Tests  2 failed | 3 passed (5)
```

After: `Tests 5 passed (5)`.

## Criteria 3 and 6 — the fallback survives, structurally

`WorkItem.assignee` is `onDelete: SetNull` and `WorkItem.reporter` is `onDelete: Restrict`. So deleting the routed member nulls the assignee column and §2's rule falls through to the reporter — who **cannot** be deleted while they report the card. The surface degrades to a different real name, never to a broken read, which is why ADR §3 is right that this column needs no denormalised label beside it. Pinned by `SURVIVES the routed member being deleted`.

## How to test

1. Sign in and open any work item with a published design result — e.g. a `design` card whose design has been published (**Design result** section, low in the item page).
2. **To see the changed line you must be a non-decider**: the sentence renders only when `canDecide` is false, i.e. you are neither assignee, nor reporter, nor a workspace manager on that project. Sign in as a plain project member who is none of those, or temporarily reassign the card to somebody else and view it as a third member.
3. **Before:** the line under the port read *"Waiting on this work item's assignee."*
   **After:** it reads *"Waiting on Mara Sandoval."* — the assignee's name, or the reporter's when the card has no assignee.
4. **Workbench → To approve** tab: expand a row whose gate you may see but not press (a project `viewer` who is the assignee). The same line in the row's frame now names the person instead of the generic fallback.
5. **Empty/edge states:** a member whose display name is blank shows their email rather than *"Waiting on ."*; a card whose routed member has been deleted falls through to the reporter's name. Neither renders the generic fallback any more unless the routing genuinely resolves to nobody.

## Checks

- `pnpm typecheck` — clean.
- `pnpm lint` — 0 errors (35 pre-existing `no-console` warnings in `scripts/*.mjs`, none in this diff).
- `tests/approval-gate-read.test.ts` 12 · `approval-gate-awaiting-me.test.ts` 23 · `approval-gate-coverage-floor.test.ts` 21 · `approval-gate-routed-to-wiring.test.ts` 5 · `approval-gate-one-language.test.ts` · `approval-gate-repository.test.ts` · `workbench-approvals-list.test.tsx` · `tests/prisma/typeBoundary.test.ts` — **all green**.
- `lib/approvalGates/routing.ts` measured at **100 / 100 / 100 / 100** (stmts / branches / funcs / lines) before being pinned in `vitest.config.ts`, per that list's own measure-then-pin rule.
- The full suite and the coverage gate are this PR's CI, which is the authority; no local full-suite run was made.

author: karl-bullock
body:
The navigation switches added in #10 could not be clicked.

They read their state from `app.data.settings` while writing to `this.setting(key)`, which is the page's unsaved buffer. Mithril re-renders on every click, the input is controlled by its `checked` attr, and that attr was recomputed from the saved value, so each click was undone by the redraw that followed it.

Both now read and write the same stream, which is the live buffer and what the save button submits.

The rate limit number fields had the identical defect: `value` came from `app.data.settings` while `oninput` wrote to the stream, so typing in them would snap back the same way. Fixed here too, since it is the same bug on the same page.

## Verified by clicking it, not by reading the markup

| step | result |
|---|---|
| fresh page | sidebar on, account on, forum nav off |
| click "Show in the forum sidebar" | stays off (this is what was broken) |
| save | persists |
| stored value | `'0'`, not `''` |
| reload the admin page | still off, no spring back |
| the forum itself | no Support link in the sidebar, still in the account menu |

The stored `'0'` and the reload are the two that matter: together they show the `Serializing` normaliser and the "only absent means default" read are both doing their job, which is the failure mode a default-on switch has in Flarum.

PHPStan and Prettier clean.

Replaces #11, which was branched before #10 was squash-merged and so conflicted on the built bundle.

body:
## Summary

Adds a way to share read-only access to a property with someone who shouldn't get a real account - a tenant, a house-sitter, a guest - without creating a `User` account for them.

- New `GuestCode` model: a short, human-friendly 8-character code (ambiguous characters like 0/O and 1/I/L excluded) tied to one `Property`, generated and collision-checked on save. Owners create and revoke codes from the property page.
- `guest_visible` boolean added to `Location`, `Appliance`, and `Guide`. Nothing is shown to a guest unless it's explicitly marked visible - existing data defaults to hidden.
- Guest login exchanges a code for a session-only guest session, expiring when the browser closes. It never calls `django.contrib.auth.login()`, so a guest never becomes a real `User` and every existing `@login_required` view stays exactly as protected as before.
- The guest property page shows guest-visible locations and appliances, with financial/registry fields (parcel number, purchase price, insurance company, etc.) left out entirely. A guest-visible appliance still shows up even if its own location isn't visible (e.g. a shared laundry appliance in an otherwise private basement).
- Guides can be linked to a property, a location, or an appliance independently. A guide shared across more than one of those is deduped on the guest page - shown once, claimed by the most specific place it appears - and the guide detail page re-checks visibility/reachability before rendering, so a guest can't view another property's guide by guessing its id.
- Revoking a code locks the guest out on their very next request.
- Owner-only nav is hidden during a guest session.
- CI's pa11y-ci accessibility scan and seed data now cover the guest login and guest property pages too.

## Testing

- Full test suite: 256 tests, 45 new (guest model, guest views, guide attaching)
- `black` / `ruff`: clean
- `manage.py check`: no issues

# PR body — feat/rivethub-opencode-theme

## Description

Generates an opencode user theme from the RivetHub desktop app's Omarchy
color snapshot, so a terminal-side opencode TUI paints with the exact
palette the app already resolves.

- `src/lib/opencode-theme.ts` — pure projector: app tokens (omarchy-theme.ts)
  → the opencode theme key set (docs key set, incl. diff/markdown/syntax
  families). `transparent` option emits `"none"` canvas/panel surfaces so the
  terminal background shows through.
- `src/lib/opencode-theme.test.ts` — 7 tests over the existing omarchy
  fixtures (osaka-jade schema-A dark, upstream-latte schema-B light):
  key coverage, token mapping, panel/selection invariants, transparent mode,
  schema doc shape.
- `scripts/rivethub-opencode-theme.ts` — CLI: reads an Omarchy
  `colors.toml` or the app's `rivethub.omarchy-theme` localStorage snapshot
  JSON, writes `~/.config/opencode/themes/rivethub-omarchy.json`, optionally
  points `tui.json` at it (`--no-set` to skip; `--out` to relocate).

## Why

opencode's built-in `system` theme only derives from the terminal when the
terminal answers OSC palette queries; behind pty proxies it silently falls
back to the opaque built-in theme and repaints the terminal background.
Feeding opencode a concrete theme file sidesteps palette detection entirely.

## Usage

    npm run theme:opencode -- ~/path/to/colors.toml
    npm run theme:opencode -- snapshot.json --transparent

- [x] No API keys, tokens, or credentials in the diff
